spec.name: abuse-protection
spec.title: Lockout and Captcha
spec.summary: Two small building blocks against password guessing and sign-up bots. IFailureLockout locks a key after repeated failures; ICaptchaVerifier checks a Turnstile, hCaptcha or reCAPTCHA token on the server. Both are registered by default and do nothing until you call them.
use: When a login or reset endpoint needs a lockout after N failures inside a time window.
When the failure budget must hold across a fleet of servers (set lockout store to backplane, which needs Redis).
When sign-up or login needs a captcha check on the server.
avoid: When you only want to cap request volume per client, use the HTTP or socket rate limits instead.
When you need to prove who a player is, use accounts-and-auth. Lockout and captcha do not authenticate.

keyTypes.summary: Locks a key (e.g. a user name plus a client address, or an address alone) after repeated failures, such as failed sign-ins. The caller picks the keys and thresholds; choose keys an attacker cannot use to lock out someone else (a user name alone can be). Default: `FailureLockout` (singleton). Thread-safe.
`altruist:security:lockout:store`: `memory` (default) or `backplane` (see `SharedCounterStore`).

A human check (captcha) for sensitive anonymous actions such as registration. Default: `TurnstileCaptchaVerifier` (singleton), configured under `altruist:security:captcha`. Expose `SiteKey` to your client and verify the widget's response token server-side before acting.

`altruist:security:captcha`: `provider` (`turnstile`, the default, `hcaptcha` or `recaptcha`: their siteverify endpoints take the same form), `site-key` (public, for your client's widget), `secret-key` (secret: from the environment), `verify-url` (another siteverify-compatible endpoint), `timeout-seconds` (10) and `max-token-length` (2048). Without a secret the captcha is off.

Server-side captcha validation against a siteverify endpoint (Cloudflare Turnstile by default): POST `secret`, `response` and `remoteip`, accept on `"success": true`. Fails closed: an unreachable or failing endpoint rejects the token (logged). Empty and over-long tokens are rejected without a call.

services.summary: The default `IFailureLockout`: sliding failure windows in memory, or with `store: backplane` a failure count per window (starting at the first failure) and the lock in the fleet backplane, so every server of a fleet sees them (memory while it is unreachable or not shared).

Server-side captcha validation against a siteverify endpoint (Cloudflare Turnstile by default): POST `secret`, `response` and `remoteip`, accept on `"success": true`. Fails closed: an unreachable or failing endpoint rejects the token (logged). Empty and over-long tokens are rejected without a call.

spec.name: connection-tickets
spec.title: Connection Tickets
spec.summary: One-time tickets that let a browser open an authenticated WebSocket without putting a long-lived token in the URL. The client trades its access token for a ticket valid for seconds, connects with ?ticket=, and the portal's [TicketShield] redeems it exactly once.
use: When a browser client connects to a portal over WebSocket and cannot send an Authorization header.
When tickets issued by one server must be redeemed by another (they live in the fleet backplane, so use Redis for a fleet).
avoid: When the client can send a header (native, TCP or UDP clients), use [JwtShield] or [SessionShield] from accounts-and-auth.
When you need a long-lived login token or a refresh flow, use accounts-and-auth. A ticket is single-use and short.

keyTypes.summary: One-time connection tickets. Browsers cannot set an Authorization header on a WebSocket, so the client trades its access token (an authenticated HTTP call of yours) for a short-lived ticket and puts it in the connection URL; `TicketShieldAttribute` redeems it on the upgrade. Tickets are 256-bit random, stored hashed in the `IFleetBackplane` (shared by every server of a fleet, so a ticket from one server works on any other) and consumed atomically on first use.

Default `IConnectionTicketService` (singleton) over the `IFleetBackplane`: keys `altruist:ticket:{hash}` hold the identity and `altruist:tickets-of:{principal}` the outstanding list; `altruist:tickets-lock:{principal}` serializes issues for one principal across the fleet, so `MaxPerPrincipal` holds under concurrency.
A one-time ticket for the client to connect with (`wss://host/portal?ticket=...`).

`altruist:security:tickets`: `query-param` ("ticket"), `ttl-seconds` (30), `max-per-principal` (4 outstanding; older ones are dropped), `session-hours` (12: the `AuthDetails` lifetime of a connection opened with a ticket) and `redact-request-logs` (true; see `TicketLogRedactionConfiguration`).
The `IShieldAuth` behind `TicketShieldAttribute`: redeems the query-string ticket of an `HttpAuthContext` (other contexts fail).

services.summary: Default `IConnectionTicketService` (singleton) over the `IFleetBackplane`: keys `altruist:ticket:{hash}` hold the identity and `altruist:tickets-of:{principal}` the outstanding list; `altruist:tickets-lock:{principal}` serializes issues for one principal across the fleet, so `MaxPerPrincipal` holds under concurrency.

ASP.NET's request log lines ("Request starting GET /game?ticket=...") contain the full URL, so the one-time ticket secret. When the application uses `TicketShieldAttribute` and `altruist:security:tickets:redact-request-logs` is true (default), only warnings of that log category (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.Diagnostics`) are kept.
The `IShieldAuth` behind `TicketShieldAttribute`: redeems the query-string ticket of an `HttpAuthContext` (other contexts fail).

attributes.summary: Shield for a portal (or controller) opened with a connection ticket: the request is rejected with 401 unless `?{query-param}=` holds a valid ticket from `IConnectionTicketService`. On success the connection's `PrincipalId` and `GroupKey` are the ticket's.

spec.name: persistence
spec.title: Persistence and the Unified Object Model
spec.summary: The data layer: model classes marked with [Vault] attributes (the Unified Object Model, UORM) map to database tables, a database provider connects to the database, and [Transactional] wraps service methods in a transaction. You write the model once and the provider creates and migrates the table.
use: When you need to store players, items or any game data in a database and describe the tables as C# classes.
When several operations must succeed or roll back together ([Transactional] on a service method).
When you want to route a model to a read replica or another database instance (DbInstance on [Vault]).
When you want to seed data at startup (IDatabaseInitializer).
avoid: When you only need fast shared in-memory or Redis state with no tables, use cache instead.
When you flush many hot, frequently changing rows, use autosave on top of the vault.
When you need to read or write rows, use vault (IVault of T). This capability is the model and provider layer.

keyTypes.summary: Seeds or prepares data after the database schema has been migrated at startup. Implement it in any loaded assembly; it is discovered automatically (no registration needed).
Base contract for a database connection provider: connection lifecycle (via `IConnectable`), connection string and keyspace (schema) management.

Low-level SQL provider: runs raw SQL with positional `?` parameters and materializes rows by property name. Used by the SQL vaults, migrations and token stores; implemented by `GeneralSqlDatabaseProvider` (Postgres: `PgSqlDbProvider`, registered as a singleton when `altruist:persistence:database:provider` is `postgres`).
A named database namespace that vault tables live in (a PostgreSQL schema).

attributes.summary: Marks a service method so that, when called through its DI-resolved service interface, it runs inside one SQL transaction: commits when the method's work has completed, rolls back when it throws.

Archives a vault table before dropping it. All data is copied to the archive table using INSERT INTO ... SELECT, then the original table is dropped. Safer than [VaultTableDelete] — data is preserved in the archive table. [VaultArchived("archived_old_stats", "Migrated to PlayerStatsVault in v3.0")] [Obsolete("Archived. Use PlayerStatsVault.", error: true)] [Vault("old_player_stats")] public class OldPlayerStatsVault : IStoredModel { ... }
Declares a class as a vault model: a persisted table. Only properties marked with `VaultColumnAttribute` become columns.
Maps a public instance property to a table column. Only properties with this attribute are persisted.

Copies data from an existing column into this new column during migration, with automatic type conversion (USING cast). The source column is NOT deleted — use [VaultColumnDelete] on a separate property to remove it after copy. Use nameof() for compile-time safety when the source property still exists, or a string literal if it was already removed from the model. // Copy int gold into new string gold_display with cast [VaultColumn("gold_display")] [VaultColumnCopy(nameof(Gold))] // or [VaultColumnCopy("gold")] if Gold property removed public string GoldDisplay { get; set; } = "";

Marks a column for deletion during migration. The column is dropped from the DB. The property serves as self-documenting history — it is ignored by the ORM (implicitly treated as [VaultIgnore]) but read by the migration planner. If [VaultColumnCopy] exists on another property referencing this column, the copy runs first, then the delete. Pair with [Obsolete] to get IDE strikethroughs and compiler warnings/errors: [VaultColumnDelete("Replaced by GoldDisplay (string) in v2.3")] [Obsolete("Column deleted. Use GoldDisplay instead.", error: true)] [VaultColumn("gold")] public int Gold { get; set; }
Creates a single-column index on this `VaultColumnAttribute` column during migration (skipped when the column is already covered by the primary key or a single-column unique key).

Drops a database column that the model no longer has a property for. Put it on the vault class, once per column; the migration drops the column (data lost) if it exists, after any `VaultColumnCopyAttribute` copy.
Declares a foreign key from this column to a column of another vault model; the migration creates the constraint. Applies only to properties that also carry `VaultColumnAttribute`.
Excludes a property from persistence even if it carries `VaultColumnAttribute`. Properties without `VaultColumnAttribute` are already ignored.
Declares the primary key of a vault model as one or more property names (composite when several). `VaultModel` already declares `[VaultPrimaryKey(nameof(StorageId))]`; apply it only to override that.

Marks a property as renamed from a previous column name. The migration planner will emit a RENAME COLUMN instead of DROP + ADD, preserving existing data. Multiple attributes can be stacked to preserve rename history — only the last one matching a current DB column is applied. [VaultRenamedFrom("original_name")] // first rename (historical) [VaultRenamedFrom("display_name")] // second rename — this one runs if "display_name" exists in DB public string PrettyName { get; set; }

Names the property used as the table's sorting column. SQL migrations create an index on it (unless it is already a primary or single-column unique key). It does not order query results; use `OrderBy` for that.

Marks an entire vault table for deletion during migration. The table is dropped from the DB. The class stays in code as self-documenting history. Apply [Obsolete] alongside this attribute to get compiler warnings/errors and IDE strikethroughs wherever the vault is injected or referenced: [VaultTableDelete("Replaced by PlayerStatsVault in v3.0")] [Obsolete("This vault is deleted. Use PlayerStatsVault instead.", error: true)] [Vault("old_player_stats")] public class OldPlayerStatsVault : IStoredModel { ... } - error: false → compiler WARNING (yellow squiggle, strikethrough) - error: true → compiler ERROR (red, won't compile if referenced)
Declares a UNIQUE constraint over one or more columns. Can be applied several times.

spec.name: vault
spec.title: Vault (IVault)
spec.summary: IVault of T is the API your code uses to read and write one table: fluent Where, OrderBy, Skip and Take, then async terminals such as ToListAsync, FirstOrDefaultAsync, SaveAsync, UpdateAsync and DeleteAsync. It also keeps a history table when the model asks for it.
use: When you query, save, update or delete rows of a [Vault] model.
When you need an audit trail of saves (StoreHistory on [Vault], then SaveAsync with saveHistory true).
When you need joins over several vault tables (IVaultJoinQuery).
avoid: When you load a root record with its related rows in one call, use prefabs.
When a hot object is changed many times a second, use autosave so the database is hit in batches.
When the data is not relational, use cache.

keyTypes.summary: Repository and immutable fluent query builder for one vault table. This is the main API for reading and writing database models.
Read-only, immutable fluent query over a vault's history table (`<table>_history`), which holds a snapshot per save made with `saveHistory: true`. Obtain it from `History`.
Contract for a row stored in a database table through `IVault`: identity, timestamp, optimistic-concurrency version and a save hook.

Base class for database-backed models. Provides the `id` (primary key), `type`, `version` and `created-at` columns; add your own `[VaultColumn]` properties and a `[Vault("table")]` attribute, then inject `IVault` to query and save it.
Process-wide catalogue of vault model types, used to resolve a model from a string type key (e.g. in admin tooling) and to enumerate all persisted models.
Immutable fluent query over a single vault table. Every builder method returns a new query; nothing runs until a terminal method (`ToListAsync`, `FirstOrDefaultAsync`, `CountAsync`).
Thrown when an optimistic concurrency (Version) check fails.

spec.name: cache
spec.title: Cache
spec.summary: A key-value cache behind one interface, ICacheProvider, with an in-memory backend (default) and a Redis backend. It holds hot or shared state such as session tokens and cross-server data.
use: When several servers must see the same state (use the Redis provider).
When tests or a single dev server should run without Redis (use the inmemory provider).

spec.name: prefabs
spec.title: Prefabs
spec.summary: A prefab is a composite entity that loads and saves a root vault model together with its related rows (single references and collections) in one call. It saves only the parts that changed, in one batched statement.
use: When a player or character is spread over several tables (account, items, equipment, guild) and you load it as one object.
When you filter by the root or by a child (Any on a collection) and eager-load only the components you need.
avoid: When one table is enough, inject IVault of T directly.
When a save must also delete removed children. Prefab saves are upserts only; delete through the child's vault.

keyTypes.summary: Loads and saves prefabs: aggregates of related vault models (one root model plus single and collection components) declared on a `PrefabModel` subclass with `PrefabComponentRootAttribute` and `PrefabComponentRefAttribute`.
Fluent query over prefabs of type TPrefab: filters on the root (and collection components via `Any`), then optionally eager-loads components.

spec.name: migrations
spec.title: Code-First Migrations
spec.summary: At every start Altruist compares your [Vault] models with the live database schema and applies the difference: new tables, columns, indexes, unique keys and foreign keys, a primary key an existing table lacks, renames and type changes. There are no migration files and no CLI. Destructive changes happen only when you ask for them.
use: When you add, rename or retype a column and want the database to follow the C# model on restart.
When you move data between columns ([VaultColumnCopy], [VaultRenamedFrom]) or retire tables ([VaultTableDelete], [VaultArchived]).
avoid: When you need hand-written SQL or a reviewed migration history. Altruist does not produce migration files.
When you only seed rows, use IDatabaseInitializer from persistence.
spec.example:
Safe by default: a column you remove from the model stays in the database with its data (a warning is logged).
Columns are dropped only with [VaultDropColumn], [VaultColumnDelete] or `drop-unmapped-columns: true`. Before
0.9.9-beta every unmapped column was dropped, so check this flag if you rely on the old cleanup.
```yaml
altruist:
  persistence:
    migration:
      drop-unmapped-columns: false   # default
      batch-size: 50000              # rows per batch while copying a column
```
```csharp
[Vault("players")]
public class PlayerVault : VaultModel
{
    [VaultColumn] public override string StorageId { get; set; } = "";

    [VaultColumn("display_name")]
    [VaultRenamedFrom("name")]          // renames the column, keeps the data
    public string DisplayName { get; set; } = "";

    [VaultColumn, VaultColumnIndex]     // added on the next start
    public int Level { get; set; }
}
```

spec.title: PostgreSQL Provider
spec.summary: The PostgreSQL implementation of the persistence layer: connection and pooling, SQL translation for IVault queries, transactions, schema isolation, prefabs and migrations. Enabled with `provider: postgres`. It is the only database provider published as a NuGet package.

`ssl-mode` defaults to `disable`. For a database outside your private network set `require`, `verify-ca` or

```yaml
altruist:
  persistence:
    database:
      provider: postgres
      host: db-primary.example.com
      port: 5432
      username: gameserver
      password: ""            # ALTRUIST__PERSISTENCE__DATABASE__PASSWORD
      database: mygame
      pooling: true
      max-pool-size: 300
      ssl-mode: verify-full
```
```yaml

altruist:
  persistence:
    database:
      provider: postgres
      instances:
        - { name: primary, host: db1, port: 5432, username: app, password: "", database: mygame, role: readwrite }
        - { name: replica, host: db2, port: 5432, username: app_ro, password: "", database: mygame, role: readonly }

Operates via raw Npgsql so callers don't have to invoke Altruist's full migration pipeline (which is keyed by `[Vault].Keyspace` at attribute level and would migrate into the production-named schemas, not the isolated copies these helpers create). spec.name: redis

spec.summary: The Redis connection and its building blocks: the shared connection factory, Redis-backed message routers and ingress/egress endpoints for multi-server pub/sub. The Redis cache provider and the fleet backplane have their own capabilities (cache, fleet-and-server-nodes) and are delivered by the same package.

When channels or servers must forward packets to each other over Redis pub/sub.
avoid: When one server is enough, use the in-memory cache (no Redis needed).
When you want a cache API, start from cache. This capability is the connection and routing plumbing.

A connection string is a StackExchange.Redis string, so Sentinel and clusters work by listing nodes. Do not put a
Redis password in config.yml; use `ALTRUIST__PERSISTENCE__REDIS__CONNECTION_STRING`.
```yaml
altruist:

      provider: redis
    redis:

spec.name: autosave
spec.title: Autosave
spec.summary: Batched, cache-first saving for vault models. You mark an object dirty and Altruist flushes dirty objects to the database on an interval, in batches, with a write-ahead log for crash recovery. It cuts thousands of single writes into a few batched ones.
use: When many players or entities change often (position, gold, stats) and writing each change would overload the database.
When a crash should lose at most a few seconds of changes (the write-ahead log is on by default).
avoid: When a change must be in the database before you continue (a trade, a purchase), call SaveAsync on the autosave service (cache and database now) or use a vault transaction.
When you only create new rows or run queries, use vault directly.
spec.example:
The interval and batch size come from the attribute first, then from config, then from the built-in defaults
(every 5 minutes, batch 100). `Wal = false` turns the write-ahead log off for low-value, high-frequency data.
```yaml
altruist:
  game:
    autosave:
      default-interval: "*/1 * * * *"
      default-batch-size: 200
      wal:
        enabled: true
        directory: data/wal
        flush-interval-seconds: 1
```
```csharp
[Autosave(120, AutosaveCycle.Seconds, BatchSize = 200)]
[Vault("players")]
public class PlayerVault : VaultModel { /* columns */ }

[Service]
public class CharacterService(IAutosaveService<PlayerVault> autosave)
{
    public Task<PlayerVault?> JoinAsync(string id) => autosave.LoadAsync(id);   // cache first
    public void Move(PlayerVault p, int x) { p.X = x; autosave.MarkDirty(p); }    // no database hit now
    public Task TradeAsync(PlayerVault p) => autosave.SaveAsync(p);               // cache and database now
}
```

Write-ahead log for a specific entity type. Buffers dirty entity snapshots in memory and periodically flushes to a dedicated .wal file. On server restart, the WAL is replayed to recover unflushed data. WAL files live in a dedicated directory (default: data/wal/), separate from app logs. One file per entity type: PlayerVault.wal, ItemVault.wal, etc. Files are self-rotating — truncated after every successful DB flush.

spec.name: fleet-and-server-nodes
spec.title: Fleet, Capacity and Drain
spec.summary: Runs one game on many servers. Every server is a node with a capacity budget, a drain (stop taking new work, let running work finish, then exit), health endpoints, and a heartbeat into a shared backplane. A fleet registry, a relay (?node=) and shared counters let a client reach the right server and let limits hold across servers.
use: When you run more than one copy of the server (Docker, Kubernetes) and rooms, lobbies or queues must find each other.
When you need a load budget (max-load), readiness and liveness probes, or a graceful scale-down on SIGTERM.
When tickets, rate limits or lockouts must be counted once for the whole fleet (shared counters in the backplane).
avoid: When you only need independent shards that never talk to each other, use multi-channel servers.
When you want to store game data, use persistence. The backplane holds only control-plane state.
spec.example:
Safe by default: the relay signs forwarded client IP headers with HMAC and ignores unsigned ones. The signing key
is `fleet:secret`, and falls back to `altruist:security:key`, so set one of them to a real secret in production.
The drain endpoint answers loopback callers; from outside it needs the `X-Altruist-Drain-Token` header, so set
`drain:token` only if you must call it remotely. The default backplane is in memory; set `fleet:redis` to share it.
Keep your orchestrator's grace period above `drain:timeout + force-grace`.
```yaml
altruist:
  server:
    http: { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 8080 }
    capacity:
      max-load: 200          # 0 = unlimited
    drain:
      timeout: 360           # seconds running work may take
      force-grace: 5
      on-shutdown: true
      token: ""              # optional, for POST /altruist/server/drain from outside loopback
    fleet:
      redis: "redis:6379"    # shared backplane (default: in memory)
      cluster: my-game       # servers with the same name form one fleet
      heartbeat: 2           # seconds
      secret: ""             # relay signature key, default altruist:security:key
```
```csharp
[Service(typeof(ICapacityContributor))]
public sealed class MyRoomsCapacity : ICapacityContributor
{
    public string Kind => "rooms";
    public CapacitySample Sample() => /* units and load of what this server runs */;
}

public sealed class Stats(IFleet fleet, IServerNode node)
{
    public string Describe() =>
        $"{node.Capacity().State}: " + string.Join(", ", fleet.Nodes.Select(n => $"{n.NodeId} {n.Load}/{n.MaxLoad}"));
}
```

keyTypes.summary: This server process as a member of a fleet: its capacity (the sum of its `ICapacityContributor`s against `max-load`) and its drain (every `IDrainParticipant` winds down before the process stops). Nothing here touches the network or the engine's hot path: allocators, autoscalers and load balancers read it through `/altruist/server/*` and the `Altruist.Server` meter.

The default `IServerNode`. Config: `altruist:server:capacity:max-load` (0 = unlimited), `altruist:server:drain:timeout` (30 s), `altruist:server:drain:force-grace` (5 s). Publishes the `Altruist.Server` meter: `altruist.server.load`, `.max_load`, `.state`, `.accepting`, `.units` and `.kind_load` (tagged `kind`).

Something that runs on this server and counts against its capacity (a room host, a world organizer, ...). Register it as a service (`[Service(typeof(ICapacityContributor))]`) or at run time with `Register`.

Something that has to wind down before the server stops: it stops taking new work when the drain begins and reports when it is done. Register it as a service (`[Service(typeof(IDrainParticipant))]`) or with `Register`.

The servers of one game as a fleet. Every server publishes itself (address, region, state, capacity, module stats) with a heartbeat and sees the others; units of work (a player's room, a lobby code) are claimed by the server that runs them, so any server can tell where they are; a player moving to another server carries its work as a `FleetHandoff`. One configuration serves one server and many: with the default in-memory backplane (or a shared one with a single server in it) every decision stays local; as soon as more servers join the shared backplane (`altruist:server:fleet:redis`) they are used, with no change to the game or its configuration.

The shared store the servers of a fleet see each other through: string values with an expiry. Only the control plane uses it (heartbeats every few seconds, a lookup when a player connects or moves); it is never on the engine's hot path. Implementations: `InMemoryFleetBackplane` (one process, the default) and the Redis backplane of `Altruist.Redis` (config `altruist:server:fleet:redis`). Keys are namespaced by the implementation.

The fleet's shared backplane on Redis (config `altruist:server:fleet:redis`, a StackExchange.Redis connection string; it may be the cache's Redis). Every server of a fleet points at the same Redis; keys live under `altruist:`. Needs Redis 6.2+ (GETDEL). A server that cannot reach Redis keeps serving on its own and rejoins the fleet when it can.

Lets a client reach a given server of the fleet through any of them, so the fleet needs one public address and no sticky routing: a WebSocket request with `?node=<id>` (see `NodeParam`) for another live server is relayed to that server's internal address, frame by frame, both ways. spec.name: game-engine
spec.title: Game Engine and Fixed-Step Loop
spec.summary: The server-side game loop. It runs your [Cycle] methods, timers and effects at a steady frame rate, and steps every registered world once per frame. A fixed-rate stepper gets whole steps of exactly 1/Hz seconds, so a simulation gives the same result however the frames fall. It is created only when the altruist:game:engine section exists.
use: When game logic must run at a steady rate (30 or 120 Hz) whatever the clients do.
When you want a [Cycle] method, a delayed effect or a cron job on the game loop.
When you need an authoritative simulation that steps at a fixed rate (for example a 60 Hz match) through IWorldStepper.
When a socket handler must hand work to the loop (WaitForNextTick, SyncCommit) instead of locking shared state.
avoid: When a [Cycle] method awaits something, do not declare it async void; the server refuses it at start. Return Task so the engine awaits it and reports its failures.

When a [Cycle] method must run once every N seconds, do not use CycleUnit.Seconds; it counts runs per second, so [Cycle(5, CycleUnit.Seconds)] runs 5 times a second. Use [Cycle(5, CycleUnit.IntervalSeconds)].
When you only need a periodic background job with no game state, and no game engine is configured. Use a plain hosted service.
When you need deterministic tick logic that the TypeScript client also runs. Write that logic with [flow] and call it from a stepper.

keyTypes.summary: The game engine loop: a dedicated high-priority thread that runs fixed-rate frames (`altruist:game:engine:framerateHz`, alias `frequency`, default 30 Hz). Each frame runs, in order: the next-tick queue (`WaitForNextTick` / `SyncCommit`), the `[Cycle]` tasks (`ScheduleTask`), the dynamic tasks (`SendTask`), the effects and one-shot timers (`ScheduleEffect`, `ScheduleOnce`, `ScheduleAtFrame`), then the world step (`WorldStep`: inline on this thread, or handed to a separate worker task). A throwing task is logged (rate-limited) and never stops the loop. Registered as `IEngineCore` when the `altruist:game:engine` config section exists; game code injects `IAltruistEngine` (a pass-through wrapper, optionally with diagnostics). The engine is started by the server once it reports alive; frames wait while the server is not alive. Threading: anything that mutates game/world state from a socket handler, HTTP request or background task should be marshalled onto the loop with `WaitForNextTick` / `SyncCommit`; slow I/O whose result the game needs goes through `RunOffTick`. For a deterministic match simulation with its own fixed step, use rooms (`Altruist.Gaming.Rooms`) rather than hand-rolled `[Cycle]` tasks. Tests: construct it with a `ManualEngineClock`, do not start it, and drive frames with `EngineTestDriver`.
Applies `IEffect` objects on the engine. A thin convenience over `ScheduleEffect` with a fixed rate; call the engine directly when you need a different rate or a plain delegate.

Runs engine frames by hand, deterministically: the engine is never started (no thread, no timer), time comes from a `ManualEngineClock`, and each frame runs the same pipeline as the live loop (next-tick queue → cycles → dynamic tasks → effects → world step). Build the engine with `world-step: inline` to have the world step inside the frame.
A clock that only moves when told to; drive the engine with `EngineTestDriver`.

Runs the independent units of one engine step (rooms, worlds) on several cores. Each unit is stepped by exactly one thread per call, so a unit's own simulation stays single-threaded and deterministic; what is shared between units must be thread-safe.
What a fixed-step clock does when a frame needs more steps than `max-steps-per-frame`.
Represents the cycle rate of an engine in different time units, calculating the number of ticks per cycle.
How the number given to `CycleRate` / `CycleAttribute` is interpreted.

spec.name: worlds
spec.title: Game Worlds and the World Coordinator
spec.summary: A world is a spatial container for game objects. It owns the physics world, the partitions, spawning and spatial queries. This capability holds the dimension-neutral parts: the world index from config, the WorldCoordinator that steps every world once per frame, the world object contracts, and the PlayerEntity base. The 2D and 3D parts are in worlds-2d and worlds-3d.
use: When you declare one or more worlds in config.yml (size, gravity, partition size, optional JSON data file).
When you spawn and look up world objects through IGameWorldOrganizer and IWorldObject.
When you want one large world with many maps, each a zone, or several separate worlds.
avoid: When you need a physics world that you own and step yourself, with no organizer, entities or visibility. Use [physics-2d].
When your game is rooms and matches rather than a persistent spatial world. Use the rooms package.

When you move a world object that has a physics body, do not assign only its Transform; the organizer copies the body's position into Transform after every step, so the object snaps back. Move the body too (body.Position, or the physics API's Teleport).
spec.example:
```yaml
altruist:
  environment:
    mode: "3D"                # or "2D"
  game:
    engine:
      framerateHz: 30
    worlds:
      partitioner: { width: 256, height: 256, depth: 256 }
      items:
        - index: 0
          id: "main-world"
          size: { x: 1000, y: 1000, z: 1000 }
          gravity: { x: 0, y: -9.81, z: 0 }
          data-path: "Resources/world.json"   # optional
```

```csharp
var world = _worldOrganizer.GetWorld(0);          // IGameWorldOrganizer3D
await world.SpawnDynamicObject(player);           // full physics body
world.SpawnLightweight(monster);                  // spatial tracking only, no body
```

spec.name: navmesh
spec.title: Navigation Mesh and Pathfinding
spec.summary: Builds a navigation mesh from a walkability grid and terrain, finds paths on it (A* plus funnel smoothing), and moves agents along those paths. NavMeshService holds one mesh per zone name. NavMeshRuntime ticks body-bound agents.
use: When NPCs or monsters must walk to a target around obstacles in a 3D world.
When you need a reachability check, a random point on the mesh, or a line-of-walk test inside a zone.
When you have a raw navmesh JSON (vertices and indices) to load.
avoid: When movement is grid-based and a walkability check per step is enough. Use [walkability-grid].
When you need a player-controlled character with slopes and jumping. Use [character-movement].

keyTypes.summary: Per-zone nav-mesh registry + query API. Games register a `NavMeshGraph` when a zone activates (typically by calling `Build` with the zone's walkability grid + terrain provider) and query paths through this service.

Central registry + ticker for body-bound nav-mesh agents. Games that want full automation (mob AI, click-to-move, patrol) register their agents here and call `Update` once per game tick — the runtime walks every agent, advances paths, and writes to the bound physics bodies. Manual-mode agents (the charge skill driving its own motion) skip this entirely.

Auto-generates a polygon nav-mesh from an `IWalkabilityGrid` + `ITerrainProvider`. The grid provides walkable/blocked per cell; the terrain provider gives Y per (X,Z). Walkable cells are greedy-meshed into rectangles to keep the polygon count low (a 512×512 cell map typically compresses to ~1–10k polys instead of ~262k tris), then adjacency is computed by scanning each rectangle's boundary cells. This is intentionally NOT a Recast clone — it can't represent overhangs or bridges that have walkable surfaces at the same XZ but different Y. For heightfield maps (Metin2-style) that's fine.

"Follow the path" runtime for an entity. Holds a current path, advances along it, and tracks whether re-planning is needed (target moved past a tolerance). Stateful per-entity; owners (mob AI, player click-to-move, charge skill) create one and tick it each frame. Two usage modes: 1. Manual. Construct with just the service + zone; the caller drives motion (reads `CurrentWaypoint`, moves the body however it wants, calls `StepToward` on arrival). This is what the charge skill uses — it has its own KCC-driven motion pipeline and just needs the path waypoints. 2. Body-bound. Construct with a physics body + speed; pass the agent to an `INavMeshRuntime` via `RegisterAgent`. The runtime ticks every registered agent each frame, sets `body.LinearVelocity` in the direction of the next waypoint, and handles arrival/replan automatically. Right shape for mob AI.

The compiled nav-mesh: an immutable polygon graph with adjacency and a 2D spatial index for point→polygon lookup. Built once per zone by `NavMeshBuilder` and consumed by the pathfinder, funnel, and services. All queries are read-only and thread-safe.

The result of a nav-mesh query: a list of waypoints from start to goal, with the polygon sequence preserved for callers that need it (e.g. agents that re-validate they're still on the expected polygon).
Parses navmesh JSON (`NavMeshSchema`) into a `WorldNavMesh`. Stateless; not a DI service.
Raw navmesh JSON (`"vertices"`, `"indices"`) read by `NavMeshLoader`.

services.summary: Default singleton `INavMeshRuntime` (registered when `altruist:game` is configured); agents are kept in a concurrent set.
Default singleton `INavMeshService` (registered when `altruist:game` is configured); one pathfinder per thread.

spec.name: terrain
spec.title: Terrain, Heightmaps and Spatial Queries
spec.summary: Answers "what is under or in front of this body?" for the character controller. With physics on, queries go to the BEPU engine. With physics off, a heightmap provider uses your ITerrainProvider (walkability, height, normal) plus the entity colliders. Also loads heightmap images (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, raw) into BEPU heightfields.
use: When you feed your own map data to the controller by implementing ITerrainProvider.
When you load a heightmap image as terrain collision in a physics world.
avoid: When physics is on and you only need ray or capsule casts. Use the physics world API in [physics-3d].
When you need paths around obstacles. Use [navmesh].
spec.example:
```yaml
altruist:
  game:
    physics:
      enabled: false
```

```csharp
[Service(typeof(ITerrainProvider))]
public class MyTerrainProvider : ITerrainProvider
{
    public bool IsWalkable(float x, float y, float z) => !Blocked(x, z);
    public float GetHeight(float x, float z) => 0f;                 // flat ground
    public Vector3 GetNormal(float x, float z) => Vector3.UnitY;
}
```

keyTypes.summary: Game-supplied terrain data (height, walkability, normal) consumed by `HeightmapSpatialQueryProvider`, the navmesh builder and the terrain-snapping body navigation helpers.
Backend-agnostic spatial queries (capsule cast, ray cast) against world 0, so gameplay code works whether or not a physics engine is running.

Physics-free `ISpatialQueryProvider`: approximate queries against an optional `ITerrainProvider` and the collider descriptors of world-0 objects. Registered as the DI singleton when config `altruist:game:physics:enabled` is `false`; otherwise `PhysicsSpatialQueryProvider` is used.

`ISpatialQueryProvider` backed by the physics engine (BEPU) of world index 0. Registered as the DI singleton when config `altruist:game:physics:enabled` is `true`; otherwise `HeightmapSpatialQueryProvider` is used.

Static heightfield terrain world object: a static body on the `Terrain` physics layer with one heightmap collider. Spawn it with `SpawnStaticObject`; its partition bounds cover the whole heightfield grid.
Facade that groups all format-specific loaders behind a single service. Usage: _heightmapLoader.PNG.LoadHeightmap(stream); _heightmapLoader.RAW.LoadHeightmap("terrain.hmap");

Regular grid of terrain height samples on the XZ plane (Y up), produced by the heightmap loaders (e.g. `IHeightmapLoader.PNG`) and consumed by heightfield colliders. Sample `(x, z)` lies at local position `(x * CellSizeX, Heights[x, z] * HeightScale, z * CellSizeZ)`.

services.summary: Physics-free `ISpatialQueryProvider`: approximate queries against an optional `ITerrainProvider` and the collider descriptors of world-0 objects. Registered as the DI singleton when config `altruist:game:physics:enabled` is `false`; otherwise `PhysicsSpatialQueryProvider` is used.

`ISpatialQueryProvider` backed by the physics engine (BEPU) of world index 0. Registered as the DI singleton when config `altruist:game:physics:enabled` is `true`; otherwise `HeightmapSpatialQueryProvider` is used.

BEPU heightmap loader: forwards the format loaders of the core `IHeightmapLoader` and builds triangle meshes for heightfield colliders. Registered in DI as a singleton `IHeightmapLoader3D` when the config section `altruist:game` is present.
Default `IHeightmapLoader` facade. Registered in DI as a singleton when the config section `altruist:game` is present; the four format loaders are injected.
JPEG luminance heights use 8-bit samples normalized to [0, 1].

16-bit PNG loader. Assumes a single-channel 16-bit grayscale heightmap (L16) with values in [0, 65535], which are normalized to [0, 1] and stored in Heights. Cell sizes and HeightScale are set to 1 by default; adjust externally if needed.

RAW loader implementing your existing binary format: [int32 width][int32 height][float cellX][float cellZ][float heightScale][width*height float samples]. This is essentially your old HeightmapLoader, just renamed and wired into the new abstraction.
TIFF heightmaps retain 16-bit sample precision, normalized to [0, 1].

spec.name: zones
spec.title: Zones
spec.summary: Zones are named rectangular regions inside a world (a town, a forest, a dungeon). Each has a position and size and must fit inside one partition. You register them on world.Zones and ask which zone contains a point. Managed zones switch on while players are in them.
use: When one big world holds many maps and you need to know which map a position belongs to.
When you want zone enter and exit logic, or zone-based entity spawning with IZoneSpawnHandler.
avoid: When you need separate physics worlds for isolated areas. Declare several worlds in [worlds].
When you need walkable-or-blocked cells inside a zone. Use [walkability-grid].

keyTypes.summary: A named spatial region within a world. Zones must fit entirely inside a single partition. Multiple zones can exist within the same partition.

Manages zone lifecycle. Zones activate when the first player enters and deactivate when the last player leaves. Choosing: use this for presence-driven spawning in persistent worlds (content exists only while someone is there). For static spatial regions with bounds checks use `IZoneManager2D` / `IZoneManager3D`; to park individual idle entities use `IEntityHibernationService`. The game reports enters/leaves; nothing calls these automatically.
Default `IZone3D`; register with `IZoneManager3D`.
Callback interface for the game to implement entity spawning/despawning. Altruist calls these when zones activate/deactivate.
A spawn definition within a zone. Game-agnostic — holds the data needed to spawn an entity. The actual entity creation is done by the game via IZoneSpawnHandler.
Thrown by `RegisterZone` when a zone is larger than a partition or does not fit inside one.

services.summary: Default `IZoneManager` (registered when `altruist:game` exists). Thread-safe. Spawning on activation is fire-and-forget (the enter call returns before the entities exist; a failed spawn is logged and resets the zone to inactive so the next enter retries); despawning on deactivation is awaited. A spawn that completes after its zone was deactivated (or deactivated and activated again) despawns what it created instead of attaching it. Without an `IZoneSpawnHandler` registered it only tracks presence.

spec.name: entity-hibernation
spec.title: Entity Hibernation
spec.summary: Parks entities that no player can see, so they stop costing tick time, and wakes them when an observer comes near. The framework hibernates zero-observer entities automatically; you decide what hibernating means for your entity.
use: When thousands of NPCs or monsters exist but only the ones near players need to be simulated.
When your entity must save or clear state when it goes to sleep (IHibernatable.OnHibernate and OnWake).
avoid: When you need to remove an entity for good. Despawn it.

keyTypes.summary: Implement on world objects that support hibernation. When no player can see this entity, it hibernates (removed from world, no AI/physics). When a player moves close, it wakes up at its last known position.

Manages entity hibernation. Entities with zero observers hibernate. When a player moves, nearby hibernated entities wake up. This is a core Altruist service that games can use for efficient entity management. The service is only a registry: removing the entity from the world on hibernate and re-inserting it after `Wake` is the caller's job, as is deciding when (e.g. from visibility). While hibernated, `IsHibernated` makes the AI service skip the entity. Thread-safe.
Default `IEntityHibernationService` (registered when `altruist:game` exists). `FindNearby` is a linear scan over all hibernated entities.
Stored state of a hibernated entity — enough to wake it later.

services.summary: Default `IEntityHibernationService` (registered when `altruist:game` exists). `FindNearby` is a linear scan over all hibernated entities.

spec.name: walkability-grid
spec.title: Walkability Grid
spec.summary: A per-zone grid of cell attributes (blocked, water, and so on) with a "can I walk from A to B" test. It is the cheap way to validate movement in grid or tile games, and it is also the input for building a navmesh.
use: When movement is tile-based and the server must refuse steps into blocked cells.
When you want to build a navmesh from the same grid.
avoid: When you need slopes, heights and sliding along walls. Use [terrain] with [character-movement].

keyTypes.summary: A 2D walkability grid for a zone/map. Each cell stores attribute flags indicating whether the cell is walkable, blocked, water, etc. Game coordinates are converted to cell indices using CellScale (e.g., cellX = gameX / CellScale).
Manages walkability grids per zone. Games register grids when zones activate.
Concrete walkability grid backed by a byte array. The game layer provides the raw data (parsed from whatever format).
Default thread-safe `IWalkabilityService` (registered when `altruist:game` exists).
Cell attribute flags for walkability grids. Games can define additional flags beyond the base set.

services.summary: Default thread-safe `IWalkabilityService` (registered when `altruist:game` exists).

spec.name: visibility
spec.title: Visibility (Interest Management)
spec.summary: Decides every tick which observers can see which world objects, diffs that against the last tick, and raises visible and invisible events. It does not send spawn or despawn packets; your game does that in the event handlers. It also feeds entity hibernation and sync broadcasting.
use: When a client should only know about entities near its player.
When you must send a spawn or despawn packet to a client at the moment an entity enters or leaves its view.
When you need to know who is looking at an entity (GetObserversOf).
avoid: When you need to broadcast one packet to everyone near a point. Use [spatial-broadcast].
When the game has no spatial world, such as a lobby or card game. Skip it.

keyTypes.summary: Tracks which world objects are visible to each explicitly registered observer. On each tick, computes the diff between previously visible and currently visible objects, then fires events for enter/leave. Observer status is explicit: call Observe(worldObject). A non-empty ClientId is still required as the network destination, but ClientId alone does not make an object an observer.
Event args for visibility changes detected by the tracker.

Default 3D `IVisibilityTracker`: each world step it computes, for every registered observer, the set of world objects within `ViewRange` (3D sphere on `Transform.Position`) and raises `OnEntityVisible` / `OnEntityInvisible` for the difference to the previous tick. Spawns and destroys are also reported immediately via the world's `OnObjectCreated`/`OnObjectDestroyed` events.

Default 2D `IVisibilityTracker` (singleton; registered when `altruist:game` exists and `altruist:environment:mode` is `2D`). Ticked by `GameWorldOrganizer2D` after physics; each tick, for every registered observer, every object of the world within `ViewRange` (Euclidean, inclusive, observer itself excluded) is visible, and the diff against the previous tick fires `OnEntityVisible` / `OnEntityInvisible` (synchronously, on the tick thread). Brute force O(observers x objects) per world; it does not use partitions. The 3D counterpart is `VisibilityTracker3D`. Observers are dropped automatically when their object leaves the world or loses its `ClientId`. tracker.OnEntityVisible += c => SendSpawn(c.ObserverClientId, c.Target); tracker.Observe(playerObject); // on join (player.ClientId must be set) tracker.RemoveObserver(clientId); // on disconnect

spec.name: spatial-broadcast
spec.title: Spatial Broadcast
spec.summary: Sends a packet only to the clients that can see an entity, using the visibility sets and the spatial hash grid. It saves bandwidth in big worlds, where most clients are far from any one event.
use: When you replicate an entity's state or event to the players who observe it.
When you need a broadcast limited to nearby partitions instead of the whole room.
avoid: When every connected client must get the message. Use the router's broadcast sender.
When you replicate an authoritative match room. Send the game's own snapshots through the rooms package.

keyTypes.summary: Visibility-aware broadcasting for persistent worlds: sends to the players that currently see an entity (the observer sets maintained by the visibility tracker). Dimension-specific variants: `ISpatialBroadcastService2D` / `ISpatialBroadcastService3D`. For match rooms, broadcast through the room instead; to reach every client use the plain router.

Lightweight, allocation-free spatial hash grid for per-tick broadphase queries. Built once per tick from the world snapshot, then queried by visibility and collision systems. Uses integer cell keys (no tuple allocation). Grid is cleared and rebuilt each tick — all internal buffers are reused across ticks (zero GC pressure in steady state).
3D broadcasting helpers: visibility-aware sends to an entity's observers (`SendToObserversAsync`) and partition-based sends around a world position.
Default `ISpatialBroadcastService3D` (also registered as `ISpatialBroadcastService`) when `altruist:game` is configured and `altruist:environment:mode` is `3D`.

2D `ISpatialBroadcastService`: besides observer-based sends (`SendToObserversAsync`, the preferred way to replicate an entity's state), it can broadcast to the clients owning objects in the partition(s) at a position. Use the spatial variants only for cheap, non-critical effects; use match-room broadcasts for room-based games. The 3D counterpart is `ISpatialBroadcastService3D`.

services.summary: Default `ISpatialBroadcastService2D` (singleton, also registered as `ISpatialBroadcastService`, when `altruist:game` exists and `altruist:environment:mode` is `2D`). Sends one packet per recipient through the router, awaiting each in turn.

Default `ISpatialBroadcastService2D` (singleton, also registered as `ISpatialBroadcastService`, when `altruist:game` exists and `altruist:environment:mode` is `2D`). Sends one packet per recipient through the router, awaiting each in turn.

spec.name: game-session
spec.title: Game Session Portal
spec.summary: A ready-made portal for the connect, handshake, join and leave flow. It creates a session per connection, answers the framework's handshake, join-game and leave-game packets, and runs registered cleanups on disconnect.
use: When you want the standard join and leave flow without writing it yourself.
When per-player state must be cleared on disconnect (implement IClientSessionCleanup).
When you want to hook into join, leave or handshake by overriding OnJoinGameReceived and friends.
avoid: When players join matches or lobbies. Use the rooms, lobbies and matchmaking packages.
When you need login and tokens. Use the auth capability.
spec.example:
```yaml
altruist:
  game:
    session:
      ttl-minutes: 60
```

```csharp
[Portal("/game")]
public class MyGamePortal : AltruistGameSessionPortal
{
    public MyGamePortal(IGameSessionService sessions, IAltruistRouter router,
        IEnumerable<IClientSessionCleanup> cleanups, ILoggerFactory loggers)
        : base(sessions, router, cleanups, loggers) { }

    protected override async Task<IResultPacket> OnJoinGameReceived(
        JoinGamePacket message, string clientId, IResultPacket result) => result;
}
```

keyTypes.summary: Base portal for the classic connect / handshake / join / leave flow: creates an `IGameSession` (keyed by the client id, TTL `altruist:game:session:ttl-minutes`, default 60) when a client connects, answers the framework's `Handshake`, `JoinGame` and `LeaveGame` packets through `IGameSessionService`, and on disconnect clears the session and runs every `IClientSessionCleanup`. When to use: derive from it (with `[Portal("/your-path")]`) when clients use the built-in handshake/join/leave packets and the socket-level rooms of `ISocketManager` (broadcast groups), typically with persistent worlds. Override the `On...Received` hooks to change the answers and the `OnSession...` hooks for your own per-connection setup and teardown. For authoritative match rooms with seats, bots and reconnects use `RoomHost` (Altruist.Gaming.Rooms) with your own portal instead; for plain per-client cleanup without this flow implement `IClientSessionCleanup`. [Portal("/game")] public sealed class GamePortal : AltruistGameSessionPortal { public GamePortal(IGameSessionService sessions, IAltruistRouter router, IEnumerable<IClientSessionCleanup> cleanups, ILoggerFactory logs) : base(sessions, router, cleanups, logs) { } protected override Task OnSessionConnectedAsync(string clientId, IGameSession session, ConnectionManager cm, AltruistConnection connection) { session.SetContext(clientId, new PlayerState()); return Task.CompletedTask; } }

Registry of `IGameSession`s by a global id (account id, user id or client id), plus the default logic of the classic handshake / join / leave packets used by `AltruistGameSessionPortal`. The default implementation is `GameSessionService` (singleton `[Service]`); replace or subclass it to change the join/leave rules. Thread-safe.

A server-side session: a TTL plus typed context objects stored under inner ids (one value per (id, type)). Thread-safe. Get one from `IGameSessionService`; `AltruistGameSessionPortal` creates one per connection keyed by the client id. When to use: ad-hoc per-player or per-connection state that should expire on its own (pending requests, selected character, temporary flags). Long-lived game state belongs in your world objects or persistence; match state belongs in the room's simulation (`RoomHost`). var session = sessions.CreateSession(accountId, DateTime.UtcNow.AddMinutes(30)); session.SetContext("party", new PartyInvite(fromId)); var invite = session.GetContext<PartyInvite>("party");
Packets produced by a session operation: some for the client, some broadcast to socket rooms.

Marker for `[Service]`s that hold per-client state and want automatic teardown when a client disconnects. Discovered at boot by `ClientSessionCleanupConfiguration` and invoked from `OnDisconnectedAsync` after the portal's own session-clear runs. One handler throwing does NOT stop the rest — exceptions are logged and the next handler still runs. Use this for any per-clientId dictionary, observer dedup set, ack table, ping timestamp, etc. — anywhere "I tracked something keyed by this client and need to forget it now." Implementing this interface plus the usual `[Service]` registration is enough; no double-tagging needed. Only connections handled by an `AltruistGameSessionPortal` trigger it; a game with its own portal (for example one driving a `RoomHost`) cleans up in its own disconnect hook instead. Named `IClientSessionCleanup` (not `ISessionService`) so it does not clash with application session types. [Service] public sealed class PingTracker : IClientSessionCleanup { private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, long> _lastPing = new(); public Task Cleanup(string clientId) { _lastPing.TryRemove(clientId, out _); return Task.CompletedTask; } }

services.summary: Discovers all `IClientSessionCleanup` implementations at DI bootstrap and registers each one as a singleton resolvable under `IClientSessionCleanup` in addition to its concrete `[Service]` registration. Lets `AltruistGameSessionPortal` inject `IEnumerable<IClientSessionCleanup>` and fan out cleanup on disconnect without users having to double-tag their classes with `[Service(typeof(IClientSessionCleanup))]`. Mirrors the shape of `ClientPacketHandlerConfig` and `CombatEventHandlerConfig` — runs during `Configure` phase, only adds factory registrations (no warmup provider, no eager instantiation). The factories resolve at runtime against the final container, so each `IClientSessionCleanup` resolves to the same singleton instance the rest of the app uses.

Default `IGameSessionService`: in-memory sessions in a concurrent dictionary (per process, not shared across servers), and default handshake / join / leave logic on the socket rooms of `ISocketManager`. Registered as `[Service(typeof(IGameSessionService))]`; the packet methods are virtual, so subclass it (and register the subclass) to change them.

config.description: Session lifetime from connect, in minutes (config `altruist:game:session:ttl-minutes`, default 60; at least 1).

spec.name: lag-compensation
spec.title: Lag Compensation
spec.summary: Keeps a short history of entity positions and lets the server rewind the world to the tick a client saw when it acted. Use it to judge hits fairly for players with latency. Live transforms are never changed; the rewind uses an override map.
use: When hit or melee validation must use where targets were on the client's screen, not where they are now.
When a packet must carry the client's tick (implement ILagCompensated).
avoid: When the client predicts and the server simulates the same fixed-step logic. Use [flow] with prediction instead.
When gameplay is not spatial or time-sensitive.

keyTypes.summary: Server-side lag compensation service. Records entity position history each tick and provides temporal rewind so any module can validate actions against where entities were at the client's perceived time. Usage — any module can wrap its logic in RewindWorld: _lagCompensation.RewindWorld(clientTick, () => { // All Compensate() calls inside here return historical positions var (x, y, z) = _lagCompensation.Compensate(entity.VirtualId, entity.X, entity.Y, entity.Z); }); Enable: set altruist:game:lag-compensation = true Configure: altruist:game:lag-compensation:history-ticks (default 64) altruist:game:lag-compensation:snapshot-strategy = nearest | interpolate (default nearest) Ticks are engine frames (`AltruistEngine.CurrentTick`); history is recorded by the 3D world organizer after each world step, keyed by the 3D world object's `VirtualId`. Not thread-safe: rewind and record on the engine/world thread. The service is optional (registered only when the config key exists): inject it nullable and use `RewindOrRun`, which simply runs the action when compensation is off. Choosing: use this for server-authoritative hit validation in persistent 3D worlds (melee sweeps, hitscan) against what the client saw. Deterministic room simulations with client prediction usually don't need it (inputs are applied at their own step instead).

Server-side lag compensation: records per-entity position history and provides temporal rewind. Opt-in via config. Any module can use this. Uses an override map during rewind — entity positions are never mutated. Entities are pushed in via `RecordSnapshot` each tick by the world organizer; the service itself doesn't depend on the organizer, which avoids a circular DI cycle when the Organizer declares an `IPositionHistoryRecorder` dependency.
How `RewindWorld` picks an entity's state at a tick (`altruist:game:lag-compensation:snapshot-strategy`).

Immutable position + yaw record at a specific engine tick. Stored in pre-allocated ring buffers — zero allocation during gameplay. Yaw is Y-axis rotation in radians; for entities without meaningful orientation, 0.

Marker interface for packets that carry a client-perceived tick for lag compensation. When the framework detects a decoded packet implementing this interface, it automatically sets PacketContext.ClientTick, enabling CombatService to rewind entity positions to the client's perceived time. Usage: [MessagePackObject] public class AttackPacket : IPacketBase, ILagCompensated { [Key(0)] public uint MessageCode { get; set; } [Key(1)] public uint TargetVID { get; set; } [Key(2)] public long ClientTick { get; set; } }

How a rewound tick between recorded snapshots is resolved.

spec.name: ai-behaviors
spec.title: AI Behaviors
spec.summary: Write a monster's brain as a plain class with [AIBehavior] and [AIState] methods. The framework finds the class, makes one state machine per entity, ticks it every engine frame, skips hibernated entities and cleans up when an entity leaves. Also has a receding-horizon planner for bots that plan ahead.
use: When NPCs or monsters need states such as idle, chase, attack and return.
When bots in a match room need the same behaviors with a machine you create and tick yourself.
When an agent must plan a short sequence of actions (RecedingPlanner).
avoid: When you need a state machine that is not AI (a door, a combo, a quest). Use [state-machines].
When bot decisions must replay exactly on a TypeScript client. Use the UtilitySelector in [flow].

keyTypes.summary: Implement on world objects that should be ticked by the AI behavior system. The service discovers the matching `AIBehaviorAttribute` by name and auto-ticks the state machine. Each engine tick `AIBehaviorService` walks the world snapshots, lazily creates one `AIStateMachine` per `InstanceId` (initialised on creation), and updates it unless the object is hibernated (`IHibernatable`), expired, or its `AIContext` is still null. Agents that are not world objects (a bot in a match room) should not implement this; create their machine with `CreateStateMachine` and tick it yourself.

AI-specific context marker over the generic state machine core. No AI-specific members here — game code defines the concrete context with whatever fields AI needs (target VID, aggro timers, wander state, …). Contexts of world objects usually also expose the entity (`IStateContext`); agents outside the world (a bot in a match room) need not.

attributes.summary: Marks a class as a named AI behavior: a set of `AIStateAttribute` / `AIStateEnterAttribute` / `AIStateExitAttribute` handler methods that `AIBehaviorDiscovery` compiles into one shared `StateMachineDef` template. Thin specialization of `StateBehaviorAttribute`. Two ways to run it: (1) world objects implementing `IAIBehaviorEntity` whose `AIBehaviorName` equals this name are ticked automatically by `AIBehaviorService` (the class is found by an assembly scan at startup and resolved from DI, falling back to a parameterless constructor); (2) agents that their owner ticks itself (a bot seat in a match room, a headless simulation, a test) call `CreateStateMachine` and drive the returned `AIStateMachine`. The behavior instance is shared by every agent: keep per-agent state in the context, not in fields. Choosing: use an AI behavior for agent decision-making with persistent states. For non-AI state machines (combos, quests, UI flows) use `StateMachineBuilder` with plain `StateAttribute`; for stateless per-tick choices use `FirstMatch` or `UtilitySelector`.

Marks a method as an AI state update handler. Thin specialization of `StateAttribute` (same options: `Initial`, `Delay`, repeatable to back several states). Signature: `string? MethodName(TContext context, float dt)` where `TContext : IAIContext`; `dt` is in seconds; return the next state's name, or null to stay.
Marks a method as a one-shot hook invoked once on transition INTO the named state (also for the initial state on `Initialize`). Signature: `void MethodName(TContext context)`.
Marks a method as a one-shot hook invoked once on transition OUT OF the named state. Signature: `void MethodName(TContext context)`.

spec.name: state-machines
spec.title: State Machines
spec.summary: A generic finite state machine for gameplay: doors, combos, boss phases, quests, match phases. State methods return the next state name. You build an immutable definition once, make one machine per context, and call Update. It has timing windows and motion curves for combos and attacks. The AI layer is built on it.
use: When something has named states with timed transitions and you want no switch statements.
When an attack or combo needs timing windows (a hit window, a cancel window) and a motion profile.
When the machine has no world entity, such as a bot in a match room.
avoid: When you want automatic discovery and per-entity ticking for monsters. Use [ai-behaviors].
When the same state logic must run bit for bit on a TypeScript client. Use [flow], which adds Advance and RunState.

keyTypes.summary: Generic FSM driver. One instance per entity. Consumers (AI service, combo system) create one from a shared `StateMachineDef` and tick it per entity. Lifecycle: build a def once with `StateMachineBuilder`, create one machine per entity, call `Initialize` once (runs the initial state's enter hook), then `Update` every tick. Time is in the same unit as the `dt` you pass (seconds by convention; durations, delays and windows assume it). Not thread-safe; the machine holds no RNG and runs handlers in a fixed order (time advance, delay gate, update, then exit → metadata → `OnStateEnter` hook → enter), so it is deterministic if the handlers are. Choosing: use this for logic with memory (phases, modes, behaviours that persist over ticks). For AI agents use `AIStateMachine` (same driver, plus discovery by `AIBehaviorAttribute`); for a stateless "which rule applies now" choice use `FirstMatch`; for scored choices use `UtilitySelector`.

Composes a `StateMachineDef` from attribute-decorated handler classes, programmatic overrides, or both. The framework loads nothing by itself — data sources (JSON, DB, config) stay in consumer code. Typical flow: var b = new StateMachineBuilder<IComboContext>(); b.RegisterHandlers<WarriorUnarmedCombo>(); // scan [State]/[StateWindow]/etc. b.ConfigureState("attack1") .Duration(1.0f) // data-driven override .Window("damage", 0.45f, 0.60f) .Data(stepDef); b.OnStateEnter((ctx, _, baseDur) => // per-domain transition hook ctx.StateDuration = baseDur / Math.Max(0.5f, ((IComboContext)ctx).AttackSpeedMul)); b.SetInitial("entry"); StateMachineDef<IComboContext> def = b.Build();

Base context for any state machine consumer. Holds the mutable per-tick values the framework needs to drive transitions and expose progress helpers. The framework sets `TimeInState`, `StateDuration`, `CurrentStateTag`, `ActiveWindows`, and `PreviousProgress` — consumer code only reads them. Not tied to a world object: a match bot, a quest or a UI flow can be driven too. `IStateContext` adds the world-entity back-reference.
First-class Altruist state-machine motion payload. Can be attached to any state and sampled by combat/locomotion code to drive damping and authored motion curves.

attributes.summary: Marks a method as a state update handler. Signature: `string? MethodName(TContext context, float dt)`, where `TContext : IStateContextCore`. Return the next state name to transition, or null to stay. The same method can back multiple states by decorating with `[State]` multiple times — different `Name` per occurrence. Use `CurrentStateTag` or builder-attached per-state data to branch. Delay: the update method is not called until `Delay` has elapsed since entry. Enter/Exit hooks still fire immediately.

Marks a class as a source of state-machine handlers. Subclasses: `AIBehaviorAttribute`, `ComboBehaviorAttribute`, etc. The attribute itself is only a marker plus a name: the framework's AI discovery scans for `AIBehaviorAttribute`; other domains derive their own subclass and feed the class to `RegisterHandlers`.
Marks a method as a one-shot hook called once on transition into the named state. Signature: `void MethodName(TContext context)`.
Marks a method as a one-shot hook called once on transition out of the named state. Signature: `void MethodName(TContext context)`.

Attaches a normalized window to a state. Multiple windows per state are allowed (e.g. "damage", "input", "cancel"). Read at runtime via `InWindow` / `WindowEntered` / `WindowExited`. Applied to the SAME method as the `StateAttribute`: [State("attack1")] [StateWindow("attack1", "damage", 0.45f, 0.60f)] [StateWindow("attack1", "input", 0.60f, 1.00f)] string? Attack1(IComboContext ctx, float dt) { ... }

spec.name: flow
spec.title: Flow (Deterministic Tick Building Blocks)
spec.summary: Small helpers for the code that runs every tick of a real-time match: ordered rule lists (FirstMatch), tick phases (TickPipeline), modifier stacks, bot utility choice, timers, input edges, entity registries and event sinks. They run in a fixed order with no allocation, and the TypeScript version behaves the same, so server and client compute the same result. It is for deterministic tick logic shared by server and client.
use: When the client predicts the server by running the same simulation, and the two must not drift apart.
When matches are replayed or rolled back and must give the same result.
When game modes or tests must insert, replace or remove one rule by name instead of copying a whole Step().
When bots must make the same choices for the same seed (UtilitySelector with DeterministicRandom).
avoid: When the server only stores state and checks requests (turn-based, lobbies, simple RPG commands). Plain code is fine.
When you need a state machine for match phases. Use [state-machines].

keyTypes.summary: Ordered rule selector: the replacement for an `if / else if` ladder that picks a result. Rules are evaluated in the order they were built; the first one that matches decides, the rest are not evaluated (their predicates never run). An optional default answers when none matched. Rule kinds: `When(name, predicate, then)` — the predicate decides; `then` produces the result.`When(name, predicate, value)` — a constant result.`Try(name, rule)` — the rule looks and may decline (returns false), e.g. a tactic that rolls a chance or latches a flag before deciding; the next rule is tried then. Determinism: the order is fixed at `Build`, evaluation is a plain loop over an array, and nothing is reordered or cached between calls. Every predicate up to the matching rule runs exactly once, in order (so predicates with side effects, such as RNG draws, consume the same sequence as the inline ladder they replace). Allocation: none per evaluation (the rules are an array of structs built once). Keep the delegates free of per-call captures (pass state through the context) to stay that way. Choosing: use this for a stateless "first rule that applies picks the value" decision re-evaluated every call; `FirstMatch` when the branches run actions instead of returning a value; `UtilitySelector` when options are scored and the best one wins (with noise and hysteresis); `StateMachine` / `AIStateMachine` when the decision has memory (a current state that persists over ticks, with enter/exit hooks and time in state); `ModifierStack` when several conditional operations combine into one float instead of one rule winning. var hitMultiplier = FirstMatch<HitContext, float>.Create() .When("super", c => c.SuperStrike, c => c.Config.SuperStrikeMultiplier) .When("kick", c => c.Kick, c => MathF.Max(c.Base, c.Config.Nose) * c.Config.FlipKick) .When("perfect", c => c.PerfectStrike, c => c.Base * c.Config.Perfect) .When("dash", c => c.DashStrike, c => c.Base * c.Config.Dash) .Otherwise(c => c.Base) .Build(); var mult = hitMultiplier.Evaluate(ctx);

The ordered, named phases of one simulation tick: the replacement for a long `Step()` method whose order is only visible by reading it. Each tick runs the steps in the order they were built; a step can be a plain action, a stop point (ends the tick early, e.g. "the world is frozen during the countdown"), or a per-entity block that runs its own sub-steps for every entity of a list, in list order (use an `EntityRegistry` for id order). Setup is editable by name (see `OrderedBuilder`): a mode or a test can insert a step before / after another, replace or remove one, without touching the rest. After `Build` the order is fixed. Determinism: a plain loop over arrays; per-entity blocks iterate the list by index (`for i in 0..Count`, the count re-read each iteration) and run every sub-step for one entity before the next entity — exactly the shape of `foreach (var v in vehicles) { stepA(v); if (skip) continue; stepB(v); }`. Allocation: none per tick (as long as the step delegates and the entity list accessor do not allocate; `List<T>` through `IReadOnlyList` does not). var vehicle = new EntitySteps<Simulation, Vehicle>() .SkipWhen("demolished", (s, v) => s.TickDemolished(v)) // true = rest skipped for v .Step("input", (s, v) => s.ReadInput(v)) .SkipWhen("frozen", (s, v) => s.Frozen) .Step("movement", (s, v) => s.Move(v)); var tick = TickPipeline<Simulation>.Create() .Step("clock", s => s.AdvanceClock()) .ForEach("vehicles", s => s.Vehicles, vehicle) .StopWhen("frozen", s => s.Frozen && s.UpdateFrozenPhase()) .Step("physics", s => s.World.Step(s.Dt)) .Build(); tick.Run(sim); Choosing: use this when EVERY step runs each tick in a fixed order (optionally stopping early); use `FirstMatch` when only the first matching branch should run.

An ordered list of float modifiers (Set / Add / Mul / Min / Max / Map), each optionally conditional, applied in order to a value: the replacement for a block of `if (a) scale = x; else if (b) scale = y; if (c) scale = MathF.Min(scale, z); if (d) scale *= w;`. Float exactness: each entry is one float32 operation applied as written (`value + x`, `value * x`, `MathF.Min(value, x)`, `MathF.Max(value, x)`) in list order — no reassociation, no folding of constants, no reordering, so the result is bit-identical to the inline code it replaces when that code applies the same operations in the same order. The operand is computed (its delegate runs) only when the entry applies, exactly like an expression inside an `if`. Choosing: use this when several conditional operations combine into ONE float (scales, gravity, speed caps); use `FirstMatch` when exactly one rule should pick the value. Conditions: `when` (optional) gates an entry. `Else` makes the next entry the `else` branch of the previous one: it is considered only when no entry of its chain applied (an `if / else if / else if` chain is one entry followed by `Else()` entries). Allocation: none per call (an array of structs built once). var gravity = ModifierStack<Vehicle>.Create() .Set("dash", c => c.Config.DashGravity, when: v => v.Dashing) .Else().Set("stall", c => c.Config.StallGravity, when: v => v.Stalling) .Min("afterglow", v => v.AfterglowScale, when: v => v.InAfterglow) .Mul("wall", v => v.WallFactor, when: v => v.OnSteep) .Build(); v.GravityScale = gravity.Apply(1f, v);

Utility-based choice between a fixed set of options (roles, tactics, targets): the replacement for a hand-written "score every role, add noise and hysteresis, take the best, then apply the exceptions" block. One `Decide` runs these stages, always in this order: Forced rules (in order): the first whose predicate is true decides at once (no scoring, no RNG draws). E.g. "kickoff until someone touched the ball".Prepare (optional): computes what the scorers share (once per decision).Scores, in option order: each option's scorer, then its veto (true sets the score to `-∞`, so no noise or bonus can pick it). The veto sees the raw score.Noise, in option order, for every option marked noisy — vetoed ones included, so the number of RNG draws per decision never depends on the situation: `score += draw(rng) * scale` (default draw: `Gaussian`). The scale is read once per decision.Inertia: the current option (unless transient) gets `heldBonus` while it has been held for less than the hold time, `bonus` after: `held = (tick - since) * tickSeconds < hold`.Best: starts from the current option (or the fallback when the current one is transient), then walks the options in order and takes any with a strictly greater score (ties keep the earlier pick).Overrides (in order): each may replace the best (they all run, each sees the previous one's answer).`Decide` does not change the current option: call `Choose` (or use `Select`, which does both) so the game can run its own "role changed" logic. Determinism: fixed option order everywhere, a fixed number of RNG draws per scored decision, float32 arithmetic applied in the order above (`score + noise`, `score + bonus`), strict comparisons. Allocation: none per decision. Choosing: use this when several options compete on a numeric score and the choice should be sticky (inertia) and optionally noisy (per-agent personality); use `FirstMatch` when a fixed priority order of conditions decides; use `AIStateMachine` / `StateMachine` for the behaviour that runs once an option is chosen (a common pattern: the selector picks a role, a state machine per role runs it). var roles = UtilitySelector<Role, BotCtx>.Create() .Force("kickoff", c => c.KickoffPending, Role.Kickoff) .Option(Role.Attack, c => c.AttackScore) .Option(Role.Defend, c => c.DefendScore, veto: (c, s) => c.NoGoalToDefend) .Noise(c => c.Personality.RoleNoise) .Inertia(c => 1.5f, heldBonus: 0.3f, bonus: 0.1f, tickSeconds: 1f / 60f) .StartWith(Role.Defend) .Build(); Role role = roles.Select(ctx, rng, tick, out bool changed);

Float timers kept in plain fields (cooldowns, windows, grace times): the named form of `t = MathF.Max(0, t - dt)` and its "just ran out" edge. Exactness: `Tick` always computes `MathF.Max(0, t - dt)` — the same float32 expression as the inline form, so a timer ticked here holds the same bits. A timer that is not running (0) stays 0. `TickRunning` only touches a running timer (the `if (t > 0) { t = MathF.Max(0, t - dt); if (t == 0) ... }` form). Choosing: use these helpers for a few timers stored as individual fields on an entity (they keep the field a plain `float`, cheap to snapshot); use `TimerSet` for an indexed group of timers ticked together (per-slot or per-pad cooldowns) that should report which ones expired this tick. Units are whatever `dt` is in (normally seconds).

An indexed set of countdown timers (pad cooldowns, per-slot respawns). `Tick` ticks every timer with `MathF.Max(0, t - dt)` in index order (exactly the inline loop) and records which ran out in this tick (`Expired`). Optional names map to indices at setup. No allocation per tick. Choosing: use this for a fixed, indexable group of timers; for one or two timers kept in fields use the `Countdown` helpers instead.

The entities of a simulation, always iterated in ascending id order (the deterministic order every per-entity loop needs), with O(1) lookup by id and O(log n) position of an id. Replaces "a list sorted after every add + a linear search by id". Order: ascending by TKey's `IComparable` (ids are unique, so the order is total and equals a sort of the list after each add). Removal keeps the order of the rest. Iteration (`foreach`, the indexer) does not allocate; adding or removing while iterating throws, like `List`.

Collects events in emission order. `Add` is an alias of `Emit`, so code written against `List<TEvent>.Add` compiles unchanged after switching the parameter type. Clear it at the start of each tick (or hand the tick's events on with `DrainTo`); the backing list is reused, so a steady tick does not allocate.

spec.name: numerics
spec.title: Numerics (Deterministic Math)
spec.summary: The math a simulation keeps rewriting: scalar clamps and approaches, angle wrapping, safe vector normalization, tuning curves, a seeded random generator, positions, rotations and transforms for 2D and 3D, box and ray tests. Each helper evaluates exactly the formula in its summary, so results match bit for bit across runs. The TypeScript package mirrors it.
