use: When a simulation must replay exactly or match a client (use DeterministicRandom, not System.Random).
When you need angle wrapping, Approach, Lerp, PiecewiseLinear curves or safe NormalizeOrZero.
When you need Position3D, Rotation3D, Transform3D and their 2D twins.
avoid: When you need operations on bodies and contacts. Use [motion-2d] or [physics-2d].
When exact repeatability does not matter and System.Numerics is enough.

keyTypes.summary: Math layer. "One number at a time" — clamp, step toward, interpolate, sign, round, quantize. Pure float32 functions, dimension-agnostic. Deterministic: same inputs give the same bits on the same runtime. Every helper evaluates exactly the expression in its summary (same operands, same grouping, no fused multiply-add), so it can replace that expression written inline without changing a bit. The TypeScript package `@altruist/sim2d` has the same functions (camelCase) with the same operation order on JavaScript numbers.

"Angle bookkeeping" — wrap, signed difference, clamped step, degree↔radian conversion, nearest equivalent angle, angular rates toward a target. Pure functions over radians. Dimension-agnostic (used identically by 2D and 3D consumers), hence the neutral namespace.

Math layer. A small, fast, seedable xorshift32 generator whose sequence is fixed forever: the same seed gives the same numbers on every runtime, machine and version, and in the TypeScript package (`@altruist/sim2d`, `DeterministicRandom`), which produces the identical sequence. Use it wherever runs must replay exactly (authoritative simulations, bots, golden tests); never `Random`, whose algorithm may change between .NET versions. Not cryptographically secure. Not thread-safe (one instance per consumer). Seeding: `state = (uint)seed * 0x9E3779B1 ^ 0x2545F491` (0 becomes 0x1234567). Step: `s ^= s << 13; s ^= s >> 17; s ^= s << 5`.

Math layer. Piecewise-linear curves given as (X, Y) points sorted by X — tuning tables, response curves, "time to reach a height" tables. Deterministic: same inputs give the same bits on the same runtime. Each segment is evaluated as `y0 + (y1 - y0) * (x - x0) / (x1 - x0)`, in that order.

Math layer. Vector algebra on `Vector2` that `Vector2` itself does not offer: safe normalize, 2D cross products, projections, components along an axis. Deterministic: same inputs give the same bits on the same runtime. Each helper evaluates exactly the expression in its summary (component by component, no fused multiply-add), so it can replace that expression written inline. The TypeScript package `@altruist/sim2d` has the same functions on `{ x, y }` objects.

A mutable 3D transform: `Position`, shape `Size`, unitless `Scale` and `Rotation`. Describes where a body/collider/world object sits and how big it is. Settable properties, plus `With*` methods that return copies.

An immutable 2D transform: `Position`, shape `Size`, unitless `Scale` and counter-clockwise `Rotation`. Used to describe where a body/collider/world object sits and how big it is. Modify with the `With*` methods, which return copies.

spec.name: physics-2d
spec.title: 2D Physics (Box2D)
spec.summary: A 2D physics engine behind a clean API. PhysxWorldEngine2D.Create makes a standalone Box2D world that you own and step yourself: bodies, fixtures, shapes, contacts and ray casts. Use it for an authoritative match, a prediction scratch world, a bot trainer or a test. Also holds the 2D collider models and body profiles that world objects use.
use: When you simulate a 2D match yourself and step it from a fixed-rate stepper.
When you need a headless physics world for tests, replays or bot training.
When 2D world objects need colliders and body profiles (box, circle, capsule, polygon).
avoid: When the game is 3D. Use [physics-3d].
When you only need velocity math or gameplay verbs on bodies. Use [motion-2d].

keyTypes.summary: Standalone 2D worlds outside the world organizer: match simulations, prediction or rollback scratch worlds. Each call is an independent, deterministic world. Threading: one world is stepped by one thread at a time; different worlds may step on different threads at once (`ParallelWorldsSupported`, e.g. rooms stepped by the engine's `step-workers`), and a world may move between threads between steps.

A 2D physics world (Box2D-backed: `Box2DWorldEngine2D`). The main entry point for standalone simulations: create bodies and fixtures, install a contact listener, step, query contacts and rays. Conventions: world units, +Y up (gravity is usually `(0, -g)`), radians counter-clockwise, seconds. Threading: not thread-safe. One thread at a time steps and touches a world (and its bodies, fixtures, contacts); different worlds may run on different threads at once when `ParallelWorldsSupported` is true (see `Box2DThreading`). Determinism: identical worlds built and stepped identically on the same runtime produce identical bits (float32 Box2D, deterministic contact order). Contact, ray-cast and per-body contact orders follow the engine's internal lists. using var world = PhysxWorldEngine2D.Create(new PhysxWorldSettings2D { Gravity = new(0, -9.81f) }); var ground = world.CreateBody(new PhysxBodyDef2D()); // static world.CreateFixture(ground, new PhysxFixtureDef2D { Shape = PhysxShape2D.Edge(new(-10, 0), new(10, 0)) }); var body = world.CreateBody(new PhysxBodyDef2D { Type = PhysxBodyType.Dynamic, Position = new(0, 4) }); world.CreateFixture(body, new PhysxFixtureDef2D { Shape = PhysxShape2D.Circle(0.5f), Density = 1f, UserData = myTag }); world.SetContactListener(new ContactRouter2D().OnBegin<MyTag, object>((in RoutedContact2D<MyTag, object> c) => { })); for (var i = 0; i < 60; i++) world.Step(1f / 60f);
DI service that creates 2D worlds (`WorldEngineFactory2D`, registered in every environment mode). Inject it where a service creates worlds; the static `Create` does the same without DI.

Settings of a standalone 2D physics world (a match simulation, a scratch world for prediction, ...). Iterations trade accuracy for speed; the defaults are Box2D's usual 8 / 3. Pass to `Create` or `Create`. var world = PhysxWorldEngine2D.Create(new PhysxWorldSettings2D { Gravity = new Vector2(0, -9.81f), // +Y up FixedDeltaTime = 1f / 60f, MaxSubSteps = 4, // opt-in fixed stepping });

A 2D rigid body (engine-agnostic). Conventions: world units, +Y up, angles in radians counter-clockwise positive (Box2D), velocities per second. Create one with `CreateBody` (standalone worlds; preferred) or, in a world-organizer setup, through `IPhysxBodyApiProvider2D`. To change its motion use the layers built on it: `BodyMotionExtensions2D` (physics layer: one velocity formula per call), `BodySteeringExtensions2D` (simple move/face/impulse helpers) and the Gaming package's `GameplayVerbs2D` (intent-level verbs). Threading: not thread-safe; touch a body only from the thread that steps its world, and not from another thread while it steps. var body = world.CreateBody(new PhysxBodyDef2D { Type = PhysxBodyType.Dynamic, Position = new(0, 2) }); world.CreateFixture(body, new PhysxFixtureDef2D { Shape = PhysxShape2D.Circle(0.5f), Density = 1f }); body.LinearVelocity = new Vector2(3, 0);
Everything a body is created with. The zero value (`default` or `new()`) is a valid definition: a `Static` body at the origin that may sleep, with a gravity scale of 1.
A shape attached to a body, with its material and filter. Pass to `CreateFixture`. Defaults: density 0, friction 0.2, restitution 0, default filter, not a sensor.

A body profile for a character: one dynamic body with a single non-trigger `Capsule2D` collider (radius = `Radius`, half length = `HalfLength`, i.e. `Size = (Radius, HalfLength)`). Note: the Box2D provider currently approximates a capsule as an oriented box of half extents (HalfLength, Radius), and `CreateBody` always returns `Dynamic` (`IsKinematic` is stored but not applied).

services.summary: The Box2D `IPhysxBodyApiProvider2D`: creates bodies in the world it is given and attaches `Collider2D`s to them as Box2D fixtures (a capsule as a box plus two circles). Stateless and shared by every world. DI: registered when `altruist:environment:mode` = `2D`. The fixtures of an attached collider get its sensor flag and user data (the `ContactRouter2D` tag), density 1 on dynamic bodies (else 0) and Box2D's default material and filter; see `Collider2D` for its events. For a material or filter use `CreateBody` / `CreateFixture`.

The `IPhysxColliderApiProvider2D` DI service: creates detached `Collider2D`s (the same as the static `PhysxCollider2D` shortcuts). The Box2D fixtures are created when the collider is attached with `AddCollider`.
Creates Box2D worlds. Registered in every environment mode (it holds no state and creates nothing until asked), so a 3D server can still run standalone 2D simulations.

spec.name: motion-2d
spec.title: 2D Motion and Gameplay Verbs
spec.summary: Two layers on top of 2D bodies. The physics layer has velocity, bounce, drag, gravity, ray cast and ballistic helpers. The gameplay layer has designer-level verbs such as JumpOff, DriveAlong, StickTo, AlignToSurface and AimAt. Each verb delegates to a physics helper, which delegates to numerics, in a fixed operation order. The TypeScript package has the same API.
use: When you write the movement of a car, ball or character in a 2D match and want the code to read like the rules.
When a client must predict that movement and match the server.
When you need to predict a flight path or check whether a jump can reach a height.
avoid: When you need 3D character movement. Use [character-movement].
When you only need pure math with no bodies. Use [numerics].

keyTypes.summary: Gameplay layer. Designer-level actions and questions on a 2D body, so game code reads like its rules (`body.JumpOff(ground, jumpSpeed)`, `body.AlignToSurface(ground, rate)`, `ball.Fall(gravity, dt, scale)`) instead of vector algebra. Layers: every verb delegates to one physics-layer operation (`BodyMotionExtensions2D`, `Velocity2D`, `Ballistics2D`, `Kinematics`), which delegates to the math layer (`Altruist.Numerics`, `Altruist.TwoD.Numerics`). Nothing is re-derived on the way, so a verb produces exactly the bits of the formula in its summary (deterministic: same state and inputs, same bits on the same runtime). Conventions: side view, +Y up, `gravity` = magnitude of the pull toward -Y; rotations counter-clockwise with the body's local +Y as its "up" (Box2D). Which layer to use. Prefer these verbs in gameplay code (rules, abilities, bot tactics) where the call should read as the intent. Drop to `BodyMotionExtensions2D` when you need a mechanical velocity operation that has no verb here, and to `Velocity2D` / `Ballistics2D` / `VectorMath2D` when you work on a velocity or position value that is not a live body's (predictions, captured contact velocities). Write raw `IPhysxBody2D` properties (`LinearVelocity`, `SetTransform`) only for state the verbs do not cover. For a side-view box body that faces left or right use `FacingFrame2D` for nose / roof / side questions. For walking characters driven by input intents use `KinematicCharacterController2D` instead of hand-writing movement with verbs. For a timed push that should keep moving the body over several ticks (knockback, dashes) without tracking it yourself use `IForceRuntime2D` (it displaces the position directly rather than changing velocity). Threading: verbs mutate the body immediately; call them on the world's tick thread (inside a step / fixed-step callback), not from network handlers. `dt` is in seconds, angles in radians. // one fixed step of a grounded body body.DriveAlong(groundTangent, targetSpeed: 12f, acceleration: 40f, dt); body.StickTo(groundNormal, acceleration: 30f, dt); body.AlignToSurface(groundNormal, rate: 10f); if (jumpPressed) body.JumpOff(groundNormal, speed: 8f); body.ClampTopSpeed(20f);

Velocity math for hand-written 2D motion and contact response: impact speed, cancelling motion into a surface, bounces, drag, scaled gravity, rigid-body point velocity. Which layer to use. These are pure functions on `Vector2` values (no body, no side effects), the velocity counterpart of the generic vector math in `VectorMath2D`. To apply one of them to a body (read `LinearVelocity`, write the result back) use the matching `BodyMotionExtensions2D` method (e.g. `Bounce` ↔ `BounceVelocity`, `CancelInto` ↔ `CancelVelocityInto`). For intent-level verbs built on those (jump, bounce off, fall, keep rolling) use `GameplayVerbs2D` in the Gaming package (e.g. `GameplayVerbs2D.BounceOff`, `GameplayVerbs2D.JumpOff`, `GameplayVerbs2D.Fall`). Conventions: side view, +Y up; normals and directions are expected to be unit length (not checked); `dt` in seconds, accelerations in units/s², drag in 1/s. For gravity, `gravity` is the magnitude (≥ 0) of the pull toward -Y. Deterministic: same inputs give the same bits on the same runtime (float32, `MathF`). Each helper evaluates exactly the expression in its summary, in that operation order, so it can replace that expression written inline. The TypeScript package `@altruist/sim2d` (`physics/velocity2D.ts`) has the same functions with the same operation order on JavaScript doubles.

Physics layer. Free flight under constant gravity, in closed form and stepped: where a projectile will be, how high it rises, how to throw it to a target, and a cheap fixed-step predictor (with an optional bouncing floor) for "where will it go" queries. Convention: side view, +Y up, `gravity` is the magnitude (≥ 0) of the pull toward -Y. Same convention as `ApplyGravity`. Deterministic: same inputs give the same bits on the same runtime. Each helper evaluates exactly the expressions in its summary. The stepped predictor is semi-implicit Euler (velocity first, then position): it is NOT bit-identical to a physics engine's integration, use the engine itself (a scratch world) when you need that. Pure functions on values (no body). The Gaming package's `GameplayVerbs2D` wraps them for a body's current state (`GameplayVerbs2D.PredictPosition`, `GameplayVerbs2D.PredictLanding`, `GameplayVerbs2D.VelocityToHit`, `GameplayVerbs2D.PredictZoneEntry`). Ignores drag and collisions (except the optional floor). Units: seconds, units/s, units/s². The TypeScript twin is `@altruist/sim2d``physics/ballistics2D.ts`. var v0 = Ballistics2D.LaunchVelocity(target - start, gravity: 9.81f, t: 0.8f); var (p, v) = Ballistics2D.Predict(start, v0, 9.81f, dt: 1f / 60f, steps: 48);

Physics layer. Velocity and angular-velocity operations on a body: each reads the body's state, applies one math-layer formula (`VectorMath2D`, `Velocity2D`, `Angle`, `Scalar`) and writes the result back (one write per call). Which layer to use. Use these when you hold an `IPhysxBody2D` and want a mechanical velocity change. Use `Velocity2D` / `VectorMath2D` directly when you work on a velocity value that is not (yet) a body's (prediction, a captured incoming velocity). The Gaming package's `GameplayVerbs2D` wraps these in intent names (e.g. `GameplayVerbs2D.PushAlong` = `AddVelocityAlong`, `GameplayVerbs2D.SetSpeedAlong` = `SetVelocityAlong`, `GameplayVerbs2D.BounceOff` = `BounceVelocity`, `GameplayVerbs2D.Fall` = `ApplyGravity`); prefer those in gameplay code. Side effects: on a Box2D body (`Body2DAdapter`) a write to `LinearVelocity` / `AngularVelocityZ` goes through Box2D's `SetLinearVelocity` / `SetAngularVelocity`, which (as in Box2D) wake a sleeping body when the new value is non-zero and are ignored by static bodies. Methods documented as "written only when ..." skip the write (and so the wake) otherwise. No allocations. Rotation convention: `RotationZ` in radians, counter-clockwise positive, as `Rotation2D` and Box2D (local +Y is the body's "up"); +Y is world up; `dt` in seconds. Deterministic: same state and inputs give the same bits on the same runtime; each method evaluates exactly the expression in its summary (float32, `MathF`). The TypeScript twin is `@altruist/sim2d``physics/bodyMotion2D.ts`, with the same operation order.
Physics layer. Ray-cast conveniences on `IPhysxWorldEngine2D`.

Physics layer. One-dimensional motion under constant acceleration: how long, how far. Dimension-agnostic (a speed along any axis). Deterministic: same inputs give the same bits on the same runtime; each helper evaluates exactly the expressions in its summary.

spec.name: collisions
spec.title: Collision Handlers and Contact Routing
spec.summary: Two ways to react to collisions. Mark a class [CollisionHandler] and its [CollisionEvent] methods get CollisionEnter, Stay, Exit, Hit and the visibility events for the two entity types you name. For a standalone 2D world, ContactRouter2D routes Box2D contacts by the types of the two fixture tags and always passes the pair in the same order.
use: When a player entering a monster's range, a pickup or a trigger volume must run game code.
When you listen to a 2D physics world's contacts and want typed handlers, filters and impulse callbacks.
avoid: When you only need visible and invisible events for packets. Use [visibility].
When you need damage rules. Use the combat package.

keyTypes.summary: Event key/payload raised on the first tick two entities begin overlapping. Carries no data.
Event key/payload raised on the first tick after two entities stop overlapping. Carries no data.

A contact listener that dispatches by the TYPES of the two tags (user data), replacing the `if (ua is X && ub is Y) ... else if (ub is X && ua is Y) ... // flip the normal` ladders of a hand-written listener. Register handlers per pair; the router orders each pair (the `TA` tag is always `A`) and orients the normal from A to B. var router = new ContactRouter2D() .FilterPreSolve<SurfaceTag, ProjectileTag>((in RoutedContact2D<SurfaceTag, ProjectileTag> c) => !PassThrough(c.A, c.BodyA, c.BodyB)) .OnPreSolve<SurfaceTag, MoverTag>((in RoutedContact2D<SurfaceTag, MoverTag> c) => { var m = c.GetWorldManifold(); // normal: surface → mover RecordSurface(c.B.Id, c.BodyB, m.Midpoint, m.Normal); }); world.SetContactListener(router); Order (deterministic, per callback): Tags are resolved (`TagOf`); a contact with a missing tag on either side is not routed.Pre-solve only: every filter whose pair matches runs, in registration order; the first that returns false disables the contact and ends the routing of this contact (no further filters or handlers).Pre-solve only: a contact without manifold points is not handled.Every handler whose pair matches runs, in registration order. Matching: a registration for (TA, TB) matches when fixture A's tag is a TA and fixture B's a TB (unswapped), else when fixture B's is a TA and fixture A's a TB (swapped). For TA = TB the unswapped orientation wins. Matching uses `is`, so base types and interfaces match their implementations. Allocation: none per contact (registrations are an array, the view is the engine's). Router vs a raw listener. Use the router when dispatch depends on what the two fixtures are (their tags). Implement `IPhysxContactListener2D` yourself only when you need every contact regardless of tags, or the engine's raw A/B orientation. A world holds one listener (`SetContactListener`); to combine, wrap the router in your listener and forward (e.g. call `PreSolve`). For per-fixture enter/stay/exit events after the step use `OnCollisionEnter` and friends instead; for polling after a step use `ContactQueries2D`. Threading: callbacks run on the thread stepping the world, inside `Step`. Register handlers before stepping; registering during a step is not synchronized. Routed contacts are views valid only inside the callback. The TypeScript twin is `@altruist/sim2d``physics/contactRouter2D.ts`.
Default singleton `ISpatialCollisionDispatcher` (always registered).

services.summary: Default singleton `ISpatialCollisionDispatcher` (always registered).
Startup configuration (picked up automatically via `[ServiceConfiguration]`) that discovers and wires up collision handlers. You normally never call it yourself.

attributes.summary: Marks an instance method (public or non-public) of a `CollisionHandlerAttribute` class as a collision event handler. The `EventType` is the logical event key the dispatcher filters on (a built-in phase such as `CollisionEnter`/`CollisionStay`/`CollisionExit`/`CollisionHit`, or any custom class, e.g. a network DTO).
Marks a class as containing collision event handlers (methods tagged with `CollisionEventAttribute`).

spec.name: physics-3d
spec.title: 3D Physics (BEPU)
spec.summary: A 3D physics engine (BEPU) behind a provider API: bodies, colliders, forces, ray and capsule casts, collision events. It is optional. Turn it off with altruist:game:physics:enabled false for games that do not need real collision, and use heightmap queries instead.
use: When the game needs real 3D collision, rigid bodies, projectile tracing or character capsule sweeps.
When you create bodies and colliders from descriptors and body profiles such as HumanoidCapsuleBodyProfile.
avoid: When thousands of NPCs only need positions and distance checks. Spawn them lightweight and set physics off, see [terrain].
When the game is 2D. Use [physics-2d].
spec.example:
```yaml
altruist:
  game:
    physics:
      enabled: true     # false: no BEPU, heightmap queries instead
```

```csharp
var profile = new HumanoidCapsuleBodyProfile(0.28f, 0.62f, 0f, isKinematic: true);
entity.BodyDescriptor = profile.CreateBody(entity.Transform);
entity.ColliderDescriptors = profile.CreateColliders(entity.Transform);
await world.SpawnDynamicObject(entity);     // creates the runtime physics body
```

keyTypes.summary: Default `IPhysxWorld3D`: a thin pass-through facade over one `IPhysxWorldEngine3D`. Threading and stepping semantics are those of the wrapped engine.
3D rigid body. Units: world units, seconds, radians; +Y is up and yaw 0 faces +Z (see `BodySteeringExtensions3D`).
Backend-specific 3D simulation (e.g. `BepuWorldEngine3D`). Obtain one from `Create`; wrap it in `PhysxWorld3D` for the engine-agnostic `IPhysxWorld3D` surface.
One hit returned by `RayCast` or `CapsuleCast`.
Engine-agnostic physics body shared by the 2D and 3D layers. Dimension-specific interfaces (`IPhysxBody2D`, `IPhysxBody3D`) add pose and velocity.

Simulation role of a physics body: `Static` never moves (infinite mass, ignores forces and gravity); `Dynamic` is fully simulated (gravity, forces, impulses, contacts); `Kinematic` is moved by code through its velocity/pose, pushes dynamic bodies without being pushed back, and ignores gravity.
`IBodyProfile3D` for an upright (local +Y) capsule character: a dynamic body tagged `Character` with one solid capsule collider.

services.summary: BEPU implementation of `IPhysxApiProvider3D`. Registered in DI as a singleton `IPhysxApiProvider3D` when the config key `altruist:environment:mode` equals `3D`.

BEPU implementation of `IPhysxBodyApiProvider3D`. Registered in DI as a singleton `IPhysxBodyApiProvider3D` when the config key `altruist:environment:mode` equals `3D`. Works only with `BepuWorldEngine3D` engines and the body adapters and colliders the BEPU providers create.
BEPU-backed collider API provider (3D). Registered in DI as a singleton `IPhysxColliderApiProvider3D` when the config key `altruist:environment:mode` equals `3D`.
BEPU implementation of `IPhysxWorldEngineFactory3D`, registered in DI as a stateless singleton. Every `Create` call returns a new, independent `BepuWorldEngine3D`.

spec.name: character-movement
spec.title: Character Controllers and Movement
spec.summary: A server-authoritative kinematic character controller. The client sends input, the controller moves the capsule each tick with gravity, ground probing, slope limits and wall sliding. Movement profiles (FPS, TPS, MMO) and abilities such as jump plug in. There is also a 2D controller, and a simpler input and output movement helper in Physx.
use: When players move in a 3D world and the server must compute the real position.
When you need walk, sprint, jump or click-to-move with different feels (profiles).
When you want a 2D character with jump abilities.
avoid: When NPCs walk paths around obstacles. Use [navmesh].
When you write car or ball motion for a 2D match. Use [motion-2d].

keyTypes.summary: Default `IKinematicCharacterController3D`: capsule character mover with camera-relative input via an `IMovementProfile3D`, yaw-only rotation, gravity, ground probing with a max slope, acceleration/deceleration, capsule collide-and-slide, depenetration, terrain snapping and pluggable `ICharacterAbility3D`s.
Server-authoritative character mover for a 3D body: takes latched movement input, applies gravity, grounding, acceleration and collide-and-slide, and writes the result to the body each tick.
Continuous (per-tick) movement input: a camera-relative move axis plus look/facing, sprint and jump. The input is latched: it keeps applying every tick until replaced via `SetMovementInput`.

Third-person `IMovementProfile3D` and the `KinematicCharacterController3D` default: camera-relative WASD where the character turns to face its move direction while moving and turns to the camera yaw when idle; external facing is ignored. Click-to-move input is delegated to `MmoMovementProfile3D`.

Minimal jump `ICharacterAbility3D`: on the rising edge of the jump input while grounded, sets vertical velocity to `JumpSpeed` and marks the character airborne. No coyote time, buffering or double jump. Holds per-character edge state, so use one instance per controller.

Default `IKinematicCharacterController2D`: a simple side-view platformer motor. Each `Step`: ray-casts down from the body's position by `GroundProbeDistance` + `SkinWidth` (any body other than its own counts as ground), runs the abilities, applies `Gravity` clamped at `MaxFallSpeed` in the air (and zeroes downward speed on the ground), moves horizontal speed toward the target with `Acceleration` / `Deceleration`, then sets `body.Position += v * dt`, `LinearVelocity = v`, `AngularVelocityZ = 0` and faces the body right (rotation 0) or left (rotation π) by the move direction. Limits: the motor teleports the body (no swept collision against walls), and the probe starts at the body's center, so `GroundProbeDistance` must cover the distance from center to feet. Not thread-safe; create one per character (not a DI service). var kcc = new KinematicCharacterController2D { MoveSpeed = 6f, SprintSpeed = 9f, GroundProbeDistance = 1.05f }; kcc.SetBody(body); kcc.AddAbility(new SimpleJumpAbility2D { JumpSpeed = 8f }); // each tick: kcc.MoveIntent(input.X); kcc.JumpIntent(input.Jump); kcc.Step(dt, world);

spec.name: combat
spec.title: Combat
spec.summary: A small combat core: one attacker hits one target, or sweeps an area (sphere, cone, line) in 2D or 3D. A damage calculator you replace turns attacker and target into damage, and hit, death and sweep events tell your game what happened. Your game keeps the formulas, rewards and packets.
use: When entities in your world hit each other and you want health, kill and event handling done for you.
When you need area attacks (cones, spheres, lines) with a target cap and a filter.
When clients send attack and target packets and you want the built-in portal gates for them.
When attacks must be checked against where targets were on the attacker's screen (it uses lag compensation when the packet carries a client tick).
avoid: When you need knockback, impulses or projectiles that move bodies. Use the physics and body APIs of the gaming package; this only moves health numbers.
When your fights are turn-based inside a match room. Put the rules in your room simulation (see rooms) and skip this service.

keyTypes.summary: Core combat service. Handles hit detection, damage application, AoE sweeps. Subscribe to events for game-specific reactions (XP, loot, aggro, animations).
Default `ICombatService` implementation (singleton via `[Service(typeof(ICombatService))]`). Resolve `ICombatService` from DI; subclass only to change sweep/damage internals.
Any world object that can participate in combat (deal or receive damage). Implement on your game's player, monster, NPC, destructible entities.
Pluggable damage calculator. Games inject their own formula. Default: attackPower - defensePower, minimum 1.

Placeholder damage calculator — used as fallback when no game-specific IDamageCalculator is registered. Games should register their own IDamageCalculator implementation via [Service(typeof(IDamageCalculator))].
Result produced by a damage calculator before it is applied to a target.
Defines an AoE shape for combat sweeps. Query semantics are controlled by `Space`: planar spaces interpret cone/line in 2D, while `ThreeD` uses full 3D volume checks. 2D analogue: `SweepQuery2D`.
Base combat portal with attack and target gates. Extend this in your game — implement ResolveAttacker and FindTarget. Override OnAttackCompleted/OnSweepCompleted for game-specific post-processing.

services.summary: Default `ICombatEventDispatcher`: reads handlers from the static `CombatEventHandlerRegistry`. Resolve `ICombatEventDispatcher` from DI rather than constructing this directly.

Startup configuration (auto-discovered via `[ServiceConfiguration]`) that registers every `CombatHandlerAttribute` class as a DI singleton and, if any were registered, adds `CombatHandlerInitializer` to wire their methods once the real container exists.
Default `ICombatService` implementation (singleton via `[Service(typeof(ICombatService))]`). Resolve `ICombatService` from DI; subclass only to change sweep/damage internals.

attributes.summary: Marks an instance method of a `CombatHandlerAttribute` class as a handler for one combat event type.
Marks a class as a combat event handler: a singleton whose `CombatEventAttribute` methods are invoked by `ICombatEventDispatcher` whenever `ICombatService` raises a hit, sweep or death.

spec.name: inventory
spec.title: Inventory
spec.summary: Items, containers and equipment for a game: grid inventories (Diablo style), slot inventories (WoW style), named equipment slots and ground items. Item types and templates are yours; the framework handles placement, stacking, moves and the client packets. The client package keeps a mirror of the server inventory in a .NET game client.
use: When players carry, stack, move, equip, drop and pick up items, and the server must be the authority.
When a .NET game client (Unity, Godot, console) needs a local mirror of the player's inventory that updates from server packets (Altruist.Client.Inventory).
avoid: When you only store a few numbers on a player (gold, level). Keep those in your own vault model and skip containers.
When the client is a browser. Altruist.Client.Inventory is for .NET clients; handle the inventory packets yourself with the typescript-client packages.

keyTypes.summary: High-level inventory service. Manages containers and provides cross-container item operations (move, equip, pickup, drop, use).
Default in-memory `IInventoryService`. Holds every container (keyed `"{ownerId}:{containerId}"`) and every tracked `GameItem` (keyed by instance id) in concurrent dictionaries; nothing is persisted.

Base class for all game items. Users extend this to define their own item types with custom properties, equipment behavior, and use effects. Apply [MessagePackObject] to your concrete subclasses for serialization.

Base item template. Users extend this with their own properties and override CreateInstance() to produce their GameItem type. Templates can be registered programmatically or loaded from JSON files (deserialized directly into the user's subclass).
Provides item template definitions. Templates can be registered programmatically or loaded from JSON (deserialized directly into the user's template subclass).

Configuration for a single inventory container, passed to `CreateContainer`. Only the fields relevant to `ContainerType` are read: Grid uses Width/Height/SlotCapacity, Slot uses SlotCount/SlotCapacity, Equipment uses EquipmentSlots. Plain POCO (not bound from appsettings by the framework).
Addresses any slot in any container. The combination of `OwnerId` + `ContainerId` identifies the storage instance (as registered in `IInventoryService`); `X` + `Y` identifies the position within it.

Base inventory portal: ready-made `GateAttribute` handlers that turn client inventory packets (`MoveItemPacket`, `PickupItemPacket`, `DropItemPacket`, `EquipItemPacket`, `UnequipItemPacket`, `UseItemPacket`) into `IInventoryService` calls and reply with an `ItemResultPacket`.

Client-side inventory mirror. Subscribes to `ItemSnapshotPacket` + `ItemSlotClearedPacket` on the dispatcher, maintains per-container snapshot cache with multi-cell coverage, and surfaces `SlotChanged` / `SlotCleared` events for UI consumers. The mirror is dimension-less until the consumer registers containers via `RegisterContainer` at boot. Snapshots arriving for unregistered windows are silently dropped — the consumer is expected to declare its layouts up front. Lifetime: registered as a DI singleton via `ClientInventoryServiceConfig`. Resolve via `Dependencies.Inject<IClientInventoryService>()` from any consumer (Unity MonoBehaviour, server-side bot, headless test). The concrete `ClientInventoryService` is only registered (and wired to the dispatcher) when `altruist:client:transport` is configured; outside DI, construct `ClientInventoryService` and pass it to `Register`. Threading: events fire synchronously on the thread that dispatches inbound packets; marshal to your UI thread if needed. Queries are not synchronized against concurrent updates. Window ids and cell indices are consumer-defined; grid cells are `y * columns + x` (see `GridLayout`).

services.summary: Forwards the `IClientInventoryService` abstraction to the concrete singleton that `ClientPacketHandlerConfig` already registered (because `ClientInventoryService` carries `PacketHandlerAttribute`). Without this forwarder, two registrations would coexist — one implicit one against the concrete type, and a hypothetical second one against the interface — and the dispatcher would call `OnItemSnapshot` on a different instance than the one consumers query through `IClientInventoryService`. We deliberately resolve the concrete singleton inside the factory so both DI keys point at the same object. Order is set high enough to run after `ClientPacketHandlerConfig` (default `0`) so the concrete singleton is registered before we forward. Runs automatically as a `[ServiceConfiguration]` step; you never call it. Like `ClientPacketHandlerConfig` it only runs when `altruist:client:transport` is configured (the concrete service exists only then), so `IClientInventoryService` is not registered without a client transport.
Default in-memory `IInventoryService`. Holds every container (keyed `"{ownerId}:{containerId}"`) and every tracked `GameItem` (keyed by instance id) in concurrent dictionaries; nothing is persisted.

Default in-memory `IItemTemplateProvider`: templates indexed by id and by case-insensitive key in concurrent dictionaries. Registered as a singleton via `[Service(typeof(IItemTemplateProvider))]`; inject the interface. Replace it with your own `[Service(typeof(IItemTemplateProvider))]` implementation to load templates from elsewhere (e.g. a database).

spec.name: questing
spec.title: Questing
spec.summary: A quest runtime. Quests are classes with attributes for id, name and requirements, and state methods that react to events such as kill, NPC talk, item pickup or timer. The runtime checks requirements, runs your hooks, saves progress and tells your game what changed. Your game owns the packets and the UI.
use: When your game has quests with steps, counters and requirements (level, class, faction).
When quest progress must survive relogs and level changes (reconcile and suspend, without deleting progress).
When you want quests as plain C# classes found by scanning an assembly.
avoid: When you only need a generic state machine for AI or entities. Use the state machine feature of the gaming package; quests add persistence, requirements and update publishing on top.
When you want a ready-made quest UI or quest packets. The package sends nothing to clients; you map QuestUpdate to your own packet.

keyTypes.summary: The quest engine: holds the registered `QuestDefinition`s, routes game events (triggers and custom hooks) to them per subject, gates them by requirements, caches and persists per-subject `QuestState` through an `IQuestStateStore`, and publishes changed `QuestUpdate`s to an `IQuestUpdateSink`.

Base class of every quest. Derive from it with your context type, decorate with `QuestAttribute`, and add behavior by implementing hook interfaces (`IOnEnter`, `IOnKill`, custom `IQuestHook` interfaces) and/or `QuestStateAttribute` methods. One instance is shared by all subjects, so keep per-subject data in `State`, never in fields.

Per-dispatch context passed to quest handlers and requirement evaluators. Games subclass it to add their own services or subject data and use the subclass as the `TContext` type argument everywhere (`QuestRuntime`, `QuestBehavior`, hook interfaces).
Game event kinds that the `QuestRuntime` routes to quests. Each built-in trigger maps to a `QuestHooks` key (see `QuestTriggerToHookKey`) and to a hook interface such as `IOnKill`.
Persistence for per-subject quest state, supplied by the game (e.g. a database repository) to `QuestRuntime`. Keys of the dictionaries are quest ids.
Receives `QuestUpdate` snapshots whenever a quest's visible status changes for a subject (typically forwards them to the client). Use `NullQuestUpdateSink` when no updates are needed.

Evaluates requirements with a given `Key` (e.g. `"level"`), comparing a game value against `Value` using `Operator`. Register in a `QuestRequirementRegistry`; for simple lambdas use the registry's `Add(key, func)` overloads instead of implementing this interface.

Snapshot of one quest for one subject, pushed to the `IQuestUpdateSink` after a dispatch (deduplicated: only sent when status, state, counter text or requirement results changed) and returned by `BuildUpdatesAsync`.

attributes.summary: Declares a `QuestBehavior` subclass as a quest with a stable, persisted id. This is the entry point of attribute-based quest authoring: decorate a class with a public parameterless constructor, implement hook interfaces (`IOnEnter`, `IOnKill`, ...) or `QuestStateAttribute` methods, and `LoadFromAssembly` discovers it.

Declares the hook key of a hook interface. Put it on an interface that extends `IQuestHook` and has exactly one method returning `Task` with a single context parameter; quests implementing it receive that hook via `FireHookAsync`. This is how custom triggers are added without changing the framework.
Alternative way to set a quest's id; consulted only when no non-blank `QuestAttribute` is present (see `Resolve`). Prefer `QuestAttribute` for new quests.
Sets the `QuestKind` of an auto-discovered quest. Defaults to `Script` when absent.
Sets the display name reported in `Name` and `Name`. Without it the CLR type name is used.

Binds a quest to an NPC key (repeatable). When `FireAsync` is called with `Npc` and an `npcKey` that has bindings, only the bound quests receive the `Npc` hook instead of every quest. Keys are matched case-insensitively; blank keys are ignored.

Gates a quest behind a requirement (repeatable; all must pass). Before every hook dispatch the runtime looks up an `IQuestRequirementEvaluator` by `Key` in the `QuestRequirementRegistry`; if any requirement fails (or has no evaluator, reason `"missing_evaluator"`) the hook is skipped and the quest is published as `Suspended`.

Marks an instance method (public or private) of a quest behavior as a handler of the named state (repeatable). Use it for multi-step quests where the same trigger means different things per step; for single-step quests the hook interfaces (`IOnKill` etc.) are simpler.

Marks a method that runs when the quest state machine enters the named state (including the lazy entry into the initial state). The method takes one context parameter and returns `void`, `Task` or `ValueTask`. Use it for one-off setup of a step (granting items, setting counters); per-trigger logic belongs in `QuestStateAttribute` handlers. One enter handler per state (last declared wins).

Marks a method that runs when the quest state machine leaves the named state, before the new state is stored. Same signature rules as `QuestStateEnterAttribute`. One exit handler per state (last declared wins).

Marks a `QuestBehavior` subclass as a behavior template that should NOT be auto-discovered as a single quest by `LoadFromAssembly`. Templates are intended to be instantiated multiple times by an `IQuestModule` — once per tier / per data row — and registered via `Register`. Only the attribute on the type itself is checked (not inherited).

spec.name: rooms
spec.title: Match Rooms
spec.summary: A host for short-lived, authoritative match rooms: a fixed group of players in an isolated instance with its own fixed-step simulation. It handles connections, seats for players and bots, ordered input, snapshots, reconnect, bot refill and room disposal. You write the simulation and the packets. Rooms are a library type, not a [Service]: you build a RoomHost yourself and expose it to the engine.
use: When your game is session-based (matches, rounds, races, arenas) and each match is its own deterministic simulation.
When you need reconnect grace, bots filling empty seats, team forfeits and clean room disposal.
When clients predict their own input and the server must apply exactly the client's input stream (see typescript-client).
avoid: When players share one persistent open world. Use the world organizers (2D or 3D) of the gaming package instead.
When you only need to group players and then start a room. Rooms alone do not queue anyone; add matchmaking (public queues) or lobbies (private invite codes).

keyTypes.summary: Hosts fixed-step, authoritative rooms: one connection per principal (the newest wins), rooms with seats driven by players or bots, sequenced inputs, snapshots on a global step phase, reconnect grace and rejoin, bot refills, the room's end and disposal. Matchmaking and lobbies plug in as `IRoomHostModule`s. A fixed-rate `IWorldStepper`: the engine's world coordinator calls `BeforeSteps`, `FixedStep` × N and `AfterSteps` every frame. Everything, including the connection calls below, runs on the engine thread (config `altruist:game:engine:world-step: inline`; post from sockets with `WaitForNextTick`). With `UseScheduler` (more than one worker) the rooms' simulation steps run in parallel inside `FixedStep`; everything else stays on the engine thread. Fleet: `UseServer` binds the host to the `IServerNode`: its rooms count against the server's capacity (kind `rooms`, load `LoadOf`), matchmaking and lobbies open rooms only while it fits, and a drain stops new rooms, lets the running ones end and finally closes what is left. When to use: session-based play (matches, rounds, races, arenas) where a fixed group of players meets in an isolated, short-lived instance with its own deterministic fixed-step simulation, and the room ends and is disposed when the match is over. For persistent, shared, open worlds that players enter and leave at will (spatial partitioning, visibility, world objects, autosave) use the world organizers instead (`IGameWorldOrganizer2D`, `IGameWorldOrganizer3D`). To gather players into rooms add `MatchmakingModule` (public queues, playlists, ratings, backfill) and/or `LobbyModule` (private invite-code lobbies whose leader starts the room) with `Use`. Setup: the host is not a DI service. The game implements `IRoomGame` (and `IRoomTransport` for sends), constructs the host, and exposes it to the engine through its own `[Service(typeof(IWorldStepper))]` class (forwarding `BeforeSteps`, `FixedStep` and `AfterSteps`, or subclassing the host). Socket handlers post `Connect`, `SubmitInput`, `Return`, `Disconnect` and `RejoinRequest` onto the engine thread. [Service(typeof(IWorldStepper))] public sealed class ArenaServer : IWorldStepper { private readonly RoomHost<ArenaSim, PadInput, Profile> _host; public ArenaServer(IAltruistEngine engine, IServerNode node, IFleet fleet, IStepScheduler scheduler) { var game = new ArenaGame(); // IRoomGame + IMatchmakingGame + ILobbyGame _host = new RoomHost<ArenaSim, PadInput, Profile>(game, new ArenaTransport(), new RoomHostOptions(), fixedHz: 60) .UseScheduler(scheduler).UseServer(node).UseFleet(fleet); _host.Use(new MatchmakingModule<ArenaSim, PadInput, Profile>(game, new MatchmakingOptions(), playlists)) .Use(new LobbyModule<ArenaSim, PadInput, Profile>(game, new LobbyOptions { Playlist = privatePlaylist })); } public StepMode Mode => StepMode.Fixed; public int FixedHz => _host.FixedHz; public void BeforeSteps(in FrameInfo f) => _host.BeforeSteps(f); public void FixedStep(in FixedStep s) => _host.FixedStep(s); public void AfterSteps(in FrameInfo f) => _host.AfterSteps(f); } // socket handler: engine.WaitForNextTick(() => host.SubmitInput(clientId, seq, input));

What the game plugs into the room host: its seat bookkeeping, bots, results and wire format. The host owns connections, seats, inputs, timing, reconnects and disposal; it never looks inside the packets. Implement it once per game (usually together with `IMatchmakingGame` and/or `ILobbyGame` when those modules are used) and pass it to the `RoomHost` constructor. Every member is called on the engine thread, except `BeforeStep`, bot `Think` calls and the simulation step, which may run on a step worker (see `BeforeStep`). Members returning a packet may return null to send nothing.

The game's authoritative simulation of one room. Single-threaded: the host calls it one fixed step at a time, on the engine thread or (with a multi-worker `IStepScheduler`) on one worker per step, never two threads at once; it may only touch its own state while stepping. Seats are identified by an int the game chooses (a car id, a slot number, ...), teams by an int. Implement it for anything a `RoomHost` runs: the host collects one input per seat (player, bot or `NeutralInput`) and calls `Step`. Determinism is up to the game (iterate seats in a fixed order, not dictionary order, if bit-identical replays matter).
Where the host's packets go (the outbound queues in production, a recorder in tests). Called on the engine thread: implementations must only enqueue, never write to a socket synchronously.

A feature on top of the host (matchmaking, lobbies). Hooks run in registration order at fixed points of the host's own flow, all on the engine thread. Add one with `Use`; implement it for a custom way of filling rooms (tournaments, scripted events) that needs the same reconnect, drain and fleet hooks the built-in matchmaking and lobby modules use. Every member has a no-op default.
Timings of the host (passed by the game; not read from configuration).
Per-room lifecycle rules (set by whoever creates the room: matchmaking, a lobby).

What a room's input is, declared by the game so the host can buffer it without knowing the game (see `InputBuffer`). Undeclared (`Opaque`), an input is a value the host may only repeat or skip when it equals the one applied before. Declared: an input has a held-buttons bitmask (`Buttons`) and everything else (axes, aim, ...) is held state too. Some buttons act when pressed (`Action`): a press is a rising edge of the bitmask. The simulation applies the presses of one step in a fixed order of stages (a jump before a dash, say); a step can hold at most one press per stage, and presses in one step happened in stage order. So an input stream says exactly which presses happened and in which order, and the buffer can: repeat the held state when a step is starved, never a press (a held button stays held: no new edge);catch up after a stall or a burst by merging two inputs into one step only when no press is lost and none changes order (`TryMerge`). Return it from `InputModel`; declare it whenever the input has buttons that act on their press, so starvation and catch-up never drop or repeat a press. public RoomInputModel<PadInput> InputModel { get; } = RoomInputModel<PadInput>.Describe() .Buttons(i => i.Buttons, (i, b) => i with { Buttons = b }) // held-buttons bitmask .Action(Jump, stage: 0) // acts on its press; applied first in a step .Action(Fire, stage: 1) .WhenStarved(i => i with { AimDelta = 0 }) // clear one-shot fields on repeats .Build();

services.summary: `/dashboard/v1/rooms`: every room host of the game (found among the world steppers, or registered as `IRoomHostInspection`) with its rooms, seats, players and module reports; operators can close a room.

spec.name: matchmaking
spec.title: Matchmaking
spec.summary: Public queues for match rooms. Waiting players are grouped by playlist (and rating), bots fill unrated rooms, and queued players can join running rooms (join in progress). It is a module you add to a RoomHost, not a [Service]; there is no config key and the options are passed in code.
use: When strangers queue for a mode (duel, 2v2, ranked) and you want them put into rooms automatically.
When you want rating windows, bot backfill or join in progress to replace leavers.
When you run a fleet and want players of one playlist to gather on one server.
avoid: When friends play together through an invite code and a leader picks the mode. Use lobbies instead.
When you have no match rooms. Matchmaking needs a RoomHost; see rooms.
When you only need the queue logic in a tool or a test without a host. Use Matchmaker alone.

keyTypes.summary: Queues, groups and join in progress on top of the `RoomHost`: waiting players first fill open (or bot) seats of running rooms that allow it — open seats at once, bot seats one at a time with a notice — and otherwise start new rooms; rated playlists group by rating window (and join rated rooms whose mean rating is inside the player's window). Everything runs on the engine thread. In a fleet (`UseFleet`) each server publishes its queue lengths; the players of a playlist gather on one server — the one with the most of them waiting that still has room (ties: the lowest server id, so every server picks the same one) — and keep their waiting time when they move. A full or draining server sends its queue on. With one server nothing moves. When to use: public queues where strangers are grouped automatically by playlist (and rating), bots fill unrated rooms and backfill seats, and join in progress replaces leavers. For friends playing together through an invite code, with a leader that picks the mode and starts, use `LobbyModule` (Altruist.Gaming.Lobbies) instead; both can be added to one host and a connection is in at most one of them at a time (`TakeOver`). `Matchmaker` alone is the pure queue logic (no host), for tools and tests. var playlists = new[] { new PlaylistOptions { Id = "duel", Mode = "1v1", TeamSize = 1, Rules = new RoomRules { JoinInProgress = true } }, new PlaylistOptions { Id = "ranked", Mode = "2v2", TeamSize = 2, Rated = true, Rules = new RoomRules { OnGraceExpired = GraceExpiredAction.Abandon, WhenEmpty = EmptyRoomAction.TeamForfeit } }, }; var mm = new MatchmakingModule<ArenaSim, PadInput, Profile>(game, new MatchmakingOptions { FillAfterSeconds = 10 }, playlists); host.Use(mm); // on a "queue" command (engine thread), after the game's own gates: if (mm.Queue.Playlist(request.Playlist) is { } playlist) mm.Enqueue(session, playlist); // on "cancel": mm.Cancel(session);
What matchmaking needs from the game; implement it (usually on the same class as `IRoomGame`) when the host uses `MatchmakingModule`. Called on the engine thread.
Timings and windows of matchmaking (passed by the game; not read from configuration).
A queue players can join: which room mode it starts, teams and their size, rated or not, and the `RoomRules` of its rooms. Passed to `MatchmakingModule`.

Queues per playlist and the rules that turn waiting players into groups. Pure (no clock, no networking): callers pass the current time. Not thread-safe. `MatchmakingModule` owns one (its `Queue`) and drives it every frame; use a `Matchmaker` directly only for tools, simulations of queue behaviour or tests.
A connection's queue status (the game turns it into its packet).

spec.name: lobbies
spec.title: Lobbies
spec.summary: Private lobbies for match rooms. A player creates a lobby, friends join by invite code, the host picks a mode and starts a room, and everyone comes back to the lobby afterwards. It is a module you add to a RoomHost, not a [Service]; options are passed in code, not read from config.
use: When friends or invited players play together (custom games, training) and a leader starts the match.
When a group must stay together between rooms and survive a reconnect during a room.
avoid: When strangers should be grouped automatically by playlist or rating. Use matchmaking instead.
When you have no match rooms. Lobbies start rooms on a RoomHost; see rooms.

keyTypes.summary: Private lobbies on top of the `RoomHost`: create or join by code, host migration, start a room with the members (bots fill the teams), return after the room, rejoin a lobby room after a reconnect. A member whose connection drops during the lobby's room keeps its place and role for the room's reconnect grace. In a fleet a lobby lives on the server it was created on and its code is claimed there: a player joining the code on another server is sent to it. A draining server moves its lobbies (members, code and host) to another server once they are not playing a room. When to use: private play among invited players (friends, custom games, training) where a leader picks the mode and starts, and the group stays together between rooms. For public queues that group strangers by playlist and rating, with backfill and join in progress, use `MatchmakingModule` (Altruist.Gaming.Matchmaking) instead; both can be added to one host and joining a lobby takes the connection out of its queue (`TakeOver`). Lobby rooms carry `LobbyCode`; their players return to the lobby (not the menu) when the room ends, and the host member's `Return` ends the room for everyone. var lobbies = new LobbyModule<ArenaSim, PadInput, Profile>(game, new LobbyOptions { MaxMembers = 6, Playlist = "private", Rules = new RoomRules { BotRefill = false } }); host.Use(lobbies); // engine thread, on client commands: lobbies.Join(session, ""); // create a lobby (the code comes back in LobbyState) lobbies.Join(session, "K7QXD"); // join by code (any server of the fleet) lobbies.Start(session, "2v2"); // host only; ILobbyGame.TeamSizeOf("2v2") must not be null
What lobbies need from the game; implement it (usually on the same class as `IRoomGame`) when the host uses `LobbyModule`. Called on the engine thread.
Settings of `LobbyModule` (passed by the game; not read from configuration).
A private group joined by invite code. The host (first member; the next one when the host leaves) picks a mode and starts rooms; after a room everyone comes back here.
One member of a `Lobby`.

Why a lobby request was refused: `NotFound` = no lobby has the code; `Full` = the lobby has `MaxMembers` members; `Unavailable` = the server cannot take it (it is draining, or full when starting a room); `TooManyPlayers` = the lobby has more members than the mode has seats.

spec.name: dashboard
spec.title: Live Dashboard
spec.summary: The operations and debugging UI of a running server, served at /altruist/dashboard with JSON APIs under /dashboard/v1. It shows config, engine, fleet, connections, worlds, rooms, caches, vaults and traffic, and it can act: edit live config, drain the server, close rooms, run SQL, call any endpoint. A VS Code extension opens the same app in an editor tab. It is off until you turn it on, and it is an admin surface that must be protected.
use: When you develop or run a server and want to see the engine, worlds, rooms, traffic and fleet live.
When you want to draw debug shapes (spawn areas, aggro radii, paths) over a world with the gizmo registry.
avoid: When you need metrics and alerts for production monitoring. Export telemetry to a monitoring tool; the dashboard is an admin tool, not a monitoring system.
When the server is public and you have not set a token or a policy. Outside Development every dashboard request is refused with 503 until you do.
spec.example:
Reference the Altruist.Dashboard package, then turn it on and protect it. Security:
- `token` is a shared secret of at least 16 characters (shorter counts as not set). Whoever has it can run SQL on your vaults, edit config, disconnect players and drain the server. Keep it in an environment variable.
- `policy` names an ASP.NET Core authorization policy you register; signed-in users who satisfy it get in. If both are set, either grants access.
- With neither set, in Development only, loopback requests (same machine) get in without credentials. `allow-loopback-without-token: false` turns that off. Requests that carry proxy headers are never treated as loopback.
- With neither set outside Development, the server still runs but every dashboard request answers 503. Nothing is exposed.
- Do not put the dashboard on the public internet without a strong token or policy and TLS. The browser login is `?dashboard_token=...` once, then an HttpOnly cookie.

```yaml
altruist:
  dashboard:
    enabled: true
    token: ${DASHBOARD_TOKEN}      # >= 16 characters; or: policy: ops
    allow-loopback-without-token: true   # Development only; default true
    network:                       # traffic recorder (on by default when the dashboard is on)
      enabled: true
      maxEvents: 10000
      maxPayloadBytes: 32768
      redactFields: [password, token, authorization]
    world:
      renderScale: 1
      terrainSampleStride: 1       # raise for large heightfields
```

```csharp
// Debug shapes over a world (inject IDashboardGizmoRegistry).
gizmos.Upsert(new DashboardGizmo
{
    Id = $"spawn:{spawnId}", WorldIndex = 0, Category = "spawns", Type = "circle",
    Color = "#F59E0BFF", Position = new Vector3Dto { X = p.X, Y = p.Y, Z = p.Z }, Radius = 4f,
});
```

In VS Code, install the altruist-dashboard-vscode .vsix and run "Altruist: Set Dashboard Token". The extension keeps the token in VS Code secret storage and reads the server address from `altruist.dashboard.baseUrl` or the workspace config.yml.

keyTypes.summary: How the Altruist dashboard (UI at `/altruist/dashboard`, JSON APIs under `/dashboard/v1`, live socket at `/ws/dashboard`) is protected, read from `altruist:dashboard:*`. Enforced by `DashboardAccessMiddleware`, which the framework installs whenever the dashboard is enabled.

Mandatory protection for every dashboard path (`ProtectedPathPrefixes`): lets a request through only with a valid token, a satisfied authorization policy, or — in Development without credentials configured — from loopback. See `DashboardAccessOptions` for the rules and config keys.

Server-side store of debug gizmos (spheres, circles, rects, boxes, polylines, ...) drawn over a world in the dashboard viewer. Game code registers gizmos by id; the dashboard pulls full snapshots over HTTP and incremental changes over the dashboard websocket.
A debug shape drawn over a world in the dashboard viewer. Publish it through `IDashboardGizmoRegistry`.

The worlds of the running game as the dashboard shows them, whatever their dimension: one implementation reads the 3D worlds (`DashboardWorldSource3D`), one the 2D worlds (`DashboardWorldSource2D`); the one matching `altruist:environment:mode` is registered.
Render hints for the world dashboard viewer, read from config and sent with every world snapshot (`RenderOptions`). Singleton DI service.
Sink for network events shown in the Altruist dashboard. The framework records HTTP requests and inbound/outbound packets itself; call it directly only to record custom traffic.
Metadata of one network event (an HTTP request or a realtime packet) for the dashboard's network inspector.

services.summary: Dashboard overview API (route `/dashboard/v1/summary`): the app's `altruist*` configuration, the registered portals/services/factories/configurations, engine settings, and live editing of config keys marked live-editable.
The dashboard's API lab (route `/dashboard/v1/lab`): lists every attribute-routed HTTP action and every registered socket gate with a sample JSON body, and lets the dashboard user invoke them.
Takes this server's `ArchitectureCardDto`: its listeners, portals and stores, as running now.

Publishes this server's `ArchitectureCardDto` to a shared fleet backplane with every fleet heartbeat interval (it lives three intervals), so any server's dashboard can draw the whole fleet, and the other fleets on the same backplane; removes it when the host stops. Does nothing with a backplane that is not shared (the dashboard then takes the card itself).

The architecture of the fleet: every server with its listeners and portals, and the databases, cache and backplane they use. Other servers are seen through the cards they publish to a shared backplane (`ArchitectureCardPublisher`), servers of other clusters on it (independent fleets, channels) too; a server of this fleet without the dashboard is known only from its heartbeat.
Dashboard controller exposing cache contents for inspection and live editing, route `/dashboard/v1/cache`. Works with both InMemory and Redis cache providers.

Listens to the engine's `Altruist.Engine` meter (`WorldCoordinator`) and keeps the last `Window` of frame and stepper timings, fixed steps and overruns for the dashboard. Listening costs a lock and an array write per measurement; it starts with the first dashboard read and stops after a minute without one.
Default thread-safe (single lock) `IDashboardGizmoRegistry`, registered as a DI singleton. Expired gizmos are purged lazily on most calls; inject the interface rather than this type.

In-process ring buffer of recent HTTP requests and socket packets for the dashboard's Network and Performance pages. The transport and HTTP pipeline call `RecordAsync`; the dashboard reads through `GetEvents` and `GetPerformance`.

Serves the embedded dashboard app at `/altruist/dashboard`: a browser UI over the JSON APIs under `/dashboard/v1/*` (server and fleet, engine, worlds, rooms, gameplay, pairing, autosave, sessions, cache, vaults, network, performance, API lab). The VS Code extension loads the same app.

Live changes of the worlds for the dashboard viewers (`GET /dashboard/v1/worlds/{index}/live`). Four times a second, on the engine thread, it compares every watched world with the previous look and hands each viewer what changed; a new viewer first gets the whole world, taken on the same thread, so its picture and the deltas fit. Nothing is compared while nobody watches; gizmo changes are always drained (so they never pile up) and passed on only when someone watches.

The 2D worlds for the dashboard: positions are (x, y) with z = 0 and rotations are about z. Objects are shown with their physics body's pose and the body's colliders (each in body space: offset, rotation, shape size or vertices). With an `IVisibilityTracker`, objects are shown only if a client owns them or someone observes them. An object spanning several partitions is listed once, under the first.

The 3D worlds for the dashboard. Objects are shown with their physics pose; when an `IVisibilityTracker` is registered, objects other than terrain are shown only if a client owns them or someone observes them. Heightfields are down-sampled by `TerrainSampleStride`, and an object that spans several partitions (terrain) is listed once.
Render hints for the world dashboard viewer, read from config and sent with every world snapshot (`RenderOptions`). Singleton DI service.

`/dashboard/v1/engine`: the game loop for operators: frame timing against the target rate, the world steppers with their clocks and timings, every `[Cycle]` task and cron job, and the failures by source.
`/dashboard/v1/gameplay`: the game services for operators: the AI behaviors and every agent's state, and the zones with their players and spawns.

Dashboard API for recorded network traffic (route `/dashboard/v1/network`). Only mapped when `altruist:dashboard:enabled` is `true`; requests must pass the dashboard protection (`DashboardAccessOptions`).
`/dashboard/v1/pairing`: phone pairing for operators: the limits and every open session with its host and companions (a session is a host screen and the phones driving it as remote pads).

Dashboard API for latency statistics (route `/dashboard/v1/performance`), computed from the events of `DashboardNetworkRecorder`. Only mapped when `altruist:dashboard:enabled` is `true`; requests must pass the dashboard protection.

`/dashboard/v1/server`: this server and its fleet for operators: capacity and drain (with the drain action), the other servers and the units they hold, the process's health, and the connection-ticket and rate-limit settings.

Dashboard controller exposing session / room information for the live transport (WebSocket / connections), route `/dashboard/v1/sessions`. Can list connections (with remote IP addresses) and forcibly disconnect clients or delete rooms.

Dashboard API for database vaults (route `/dashboard/v1/vaults`): lists registered vault models with their columns, pages through rows, edits rows by primary key, and runs raw SQL against SQL-backed (PostgreSQL) vaults.

The world viewer's HTTP API under `/dashboard/v1/worlds`, for 2D and 3D worlds alike (`IDashboardWorldSource`): list the worlds, load one in full, inspect an object, and follow a world live as an NDJSON stream of `DashboardWorldDelta`s.

spec.name: dotnet-client
spec.title: .NET Client
spec.summary: A client library for talking to an Altruist server from .NET: Unity, Godot, Blazor, console tools and test harnesses. It speaks the server's wire protocol over TCP, UDP or WebSocket with a MessagePack or JSON codec, and dispatches incoming packets to methods marked [Packet]. Transports are chosen in config.
use: When a .NET program (Unity, Godot, a bot, a load test) must connect to an Altruist server.
When you want one router that sends by gate name and can pick TCP, UDP or WebSocket per message.
When incoming packets should be routed by message code to your handler methods.
avoid: When the client is a browser game. Use the typescript-client packages instead.
When you write end-to-end tests of your own server in the same repo. Use the testing capability (Altruist.Testing); it has test clients with the same shape.

keyTypes.summary: Client-side counterpart of the server's `IAltruistRouter`. Single DI service that user code injects to send packets and observe connection lifecycle. The transport implementations themselves (`AltruistTcpClient`, `AltruistUdpClient`, `AltruistWebSocketClient`) are `internal` and never directly injected — the router owns them. Send patterns: `router.SendAsync(gate, packet)` — uses `ClientTransportConfig.DefaultTransport`.`router.Tcp.SendAsync(gate, packet)` / `router.Udp.SendAsync(...)` / `router.Ws.SendAsync(...)` — picks the transport explicitly. Lifecycle:`ConnectAsync` brings up every transport declared in `ClientTransportConfig`; `OnConnected` fires once after all configured transports finish their handshakes. `OnDisconnected` fires when any configured transport drops; a re-connect needs an explicit `ConnectAsync` from the consumer. Bound from the `altruist:client:transport` section of `config.yml`. Mirrors the server's `altruist:server:transport` shape — same vocabulary, same binding pattern, so a developer who knows the server config doesn't need to learn anything new. Pluggable codec contract. Default impl is `MessagePackClientCodec`; JSON is offered for browser/WebSocket scenarios. Consumers can ship their own. Unity-shape.`DrainAsync` awaits inbound frames inside `timeout` and returns them. Test-shape. Concurrency:`SendAsync` locks the underlying stream so multi-thread send won't interleave bytes (we caught a real bug in production from this; `ConcurrentSendTests` is the regression guard). Internal: application code sends through `IAltruistClientRouter` / `ITransportSender`, which own this instance. Registered as a DI singleton only when `altruist:client:transport:tcp` is configured.

UDP client speaking the Altruist wire protocol. UDP datagrams are inherently framed, so there's no length prefix. Outbound: `[1 byte gateLen][gate UTF-8][codec(packet)]`. Inbound: server sends a codec-encoded `MessageEnvelope` per datagram. Use for high-frequency lossy traffic — movement deltas, voice, etc. Server identifies the client by source endpoint; no handshake. Internal: send through `Udp`. Registered as a DI singleton only when `altruist:client:transport:udp` is configured.

WebSocket client for the Altruist wire protocol. Frames are messages — no length prefix needed. Outbound frames have the shape the server's read loop parses: binary codecs send `[u8 gateLength][gate UTF-8][codec(payload)]` (like TCP and UDP), the JSON codec sends the text frame `{"event": gate, "data": payload}`. JSON codec → text frames; any other codec → binary frames. Internal: send through `Ws`. Registered as a DI singleton only when `altruist:client:transport:ws` is configured; the URL comes from `WebSocketUri` (plain `ws`, or TLS `wss` with `secure: true`).

Picks an `IClientCodec` by its `Provider` name. DI populates the candidate set with every `IClientCodec` registered via `[Service(typeof(IClientCodec))]`; the router asks for "messagepack" or "json" based on the `config.yml` codec block. Mirrors the server's `CodecResolver` shape so a developer who configures the server already knows how to configure the client. DI singleton (`[Service]`). Inject it only when building transports or codecs by hand; normal client code never needs it.

Routes inbound server frames to `PacketAttribute`-decorated handler methods. Mirrors the server's `CombatEventDispatcher` shape: assembly scan → per-method `Expression.Lambda` compile → registry keyed off the packet's auto-detected `MessageCode`. The wire shape is the standard `MessageEnvelope` fixarray(3) — element [0] is the MessageCode, element [2] is the inner packet bytes. We peek the MC via `MessageEnvelopeShape` (no MessagePack on the envelope), look up registered handlers, then call the codec's `Deserialize<T>` with the slice and invoke every handler. The codec is supplied per-call rather than at construction — different transports may use different codecs (e.g. TCP+messagepack, WS+JSON), and the same dispatcher serves all of them. Multiple `PacketAttribute` methods MAY register for the same packet type; all of them fire on dispatch. Order is undefined — if the game ever needs ordering we add an `Order` property to the attribute. Errors are caught and routed through `Logger` so one bad packet or buggy handler doesn't crash the receive loop. Logger is null by default (silent). Wire format: a codec implementing `IClientEnvelopeCodec` (such as `JsonClientCodec`) reads the envelope itself; for every other codec it is parsed as MessagePack (`MessageEnvelopeShape`). Only the inner packet goes through the codec's `Deserialize<T>`. Threading: handlers run synchronously on whatever thread calls `Dispatch` — a background pump task when the router auto-pumps, or the caller of `DrainInbound` otherwise. `Register` is safe to call concurrently with dispatch. Lifetime: DI singleton (`[Service]`). attributes.summary: Method-level marker on a `PacketHandlerAttribute`-decorated class declaring "this method handles packets of type `packetType`". Mirrors the server's `[CombatEvent(typeof(X))]` shape. Multiple methods MAY register for the same packet type — every matching handler is invoked on dispatch (multi-sub). The wire `MessageCode` is auto-detected by reading `MessageCode` from a default instance of `packetType`, so the packet itself remains the single source of truth for routing. The method must be a public or non-public instance method returning `void` with exactly one parameter whose type equals `PacketType`; violations throw from `Register`. Handlers run on the dispatching thread (see `ClientPacketDispatcher`).

Class-level marker for a class that contains `PacketAttribute`-annotated methods. Mirrors the server's `[CombatHandler]` opt-in convention — only classes with this marker are discovered at boot by `ClientPacketHandlerConfig`, which registers them as DI singletons and passes the instance to `Register`. The discovery step registers the class itself, so `[Service]` is optional (add it only if you also want it exposed under an interface). Constructor dependencies must be resolvable from DI, otherwise the class is skipped with a debug log. Discovery only runs when `altruist:client:transport` is configured. Outside DI, skip this attribute and call `Register` directly. [Service] [PacketHandler] public sealed class GameHandlers { [Packet(typeof(DamageInfo))] public void OnDamage(DamageInfo dmg) { ... } }

spec.name: typescript-client
spec.title: TypeScript Client SDK
spec.summary: Dependency-free TypeScript packages for browser game clients. @altruist/net has the MessagePack wire format, the WebSocket transport (tickets, reconnect, heartbeat, fleet redirect) and ping and clock diagnostics. @altruist/client adds HTTP auth, the matchmaking and lobby flow, and device pairing. @altruist/input and @altruist/prediction match the server's room input and fixed-step clock, so the client can predict its own player exactly.
use: When a browser game connects to an Altruist server and you want the socket, token refresh and packet routing done.
When the game queues or joins lobbies and you want the phase machine that mirrors MatchmakingModule and LobbyModule.
When the client predicts its own movement against a RoomHost and must send inputs in the order and rate the server's input buffer expects.
avoid: When the client is .NET (Unity, Godot, console). Use the dotnet-client package.
When you only need the 2D physics and gameplay helpers to run the same simulation in the browser. That is typescript-sim2d.

spec.name: typescript-sim2d
spec.title: TypeScript 2D Simulation and AI
spec.summary: TypeScript twins of Altruist's 2D math, physics, gameplay verbs and flow building blocks (@altruist/sim2d), and of its receding-horizon game AI planner (@altruist/ai). They follow the C# operation order, so a browser client can run the same simulation as the server for prediction, replays, offline play and bots.
use: When the browser must reproduce server physics or gameplay exactly (client-side prediction, replays).
When you run bots or offline play in the browser using the same rules as the server.
When you want an anytime planner that scores candidate input programs by rolling out your own simulation (@altruist/ai).
avoid: When you only need sockets, auth or matchmaking in the browser. Use typescript-client.
When the simulation does not need to match the server. Use your own physics library; sim2d is for deterministic twins.
